verses.translation: We must learn that truth may be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, and that each of these ways is true as far as it goes. … God is like that water filling these different vessels, and in each vessel the vision of God comes in the form of the vessel.
verses.line: truth may be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, and that each of these ways is true as far as it goes.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Ideal of a Universal Religion, p. 385
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion', America, on how anyone grows.
verses.translation: Do you think you can teach even a child? You cannot. The child teaches himself. Your duty is to afford opportunities and to remove obstacles. A plant grows. Do you make the plant grow? Your duty is to put a hedge round it and see that no animal eats up the plant, and there your duty ends.
verses.line: Your duty is to afford opportunities and to remove obstacles.
verses.misuse: Not 'leave children to it'; protecting and providing is the hedge he describes.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Ideal of a Universal Religion, p. 385
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion', America: his plan, 'Do not destroy'.
verses.translation: Help, if you can; if you cannot, fold your hands and stand by and see things go on. Do not injure, if you cannot render help. Say not a word against any man's convictions so far as they are sincere.
verses.line: Say not a word against any man's convictions so far as they are sincere.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Ideal of a Universal Religion, p. 385
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion', America.
verses.translation: None can teach you; none can make a spiritual man of you. You have to teach yourself; your growth must come from inside.
verses.line: You have to teach yourself; your growth must come from inside.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion, p. 365
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion', Universalist Church, Pasadena, 28 January 1900.
verses.translation: Thinking beings must differ; difference is the first sign of thought. If I am a thoughtful man, certainly I ought to like to live amongst thoughtful persons where there are differences of opinion.
verses.line: Thinking beings must differ; difference is the first sign of thought.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion, p. 369
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion', Universalist Church, Pasadena, 28 January 1900.
verses.translation: Not only must you have the spiritual ideas, but they must come to you according to your own method. They must speak your own language, the language of your soul, and then alone they will satisfy you.
verses.line: They must speak your own language, the language of your soul,

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: God in Everything, p. 153
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'God in Everything', London, 27 October 1896.
verses.translation: Never mind failures; they are quite natural, they are the beauty of life, these failures. What would life be without them? It would not be worth having if it were not for struggles. Where would be the poetry of life? Never mind the struggles, the mistakes. I never heard a cow tell a lie, but it is only a cow — never a man. So never mind these failures, these little backslidings; hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, make the attempt once more.
verses.line: hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, make the attempt once more.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: Realisation, p. 170
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'Realisation', London, 29 October 1896, reading the Katha Upanishad.
verses.translation: It is, as it were, walking on the edge of a razor; the way is long and perilous, but struggle on, do not despair. Awake, arise, and stop not till the goal is reached.
verses.line: the way is long and perilous, but struggle on, do not despair.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: The Cosmos: the Microcosm, p. 225
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Cosmos: The Microcosm', New York, 26 January 1896.
verses.translation: Therefore, stand up, be bold, be strong. Take the whole responsibility on your own shoulders, and know that you are the creator of your own destiny. All the strength and succour you want is within yourselves. Therefore, make your own future.
verses.line: know that you are the creator of your own destiny.
verses.misuse: Not 'everything that happens to you is your doing'; it is about what you build from here.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Address of Welcome Presented at Calcutta and Reply, p. 321
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Reply to the Calcutta welcome, 28 February 1897, his homecoming after America.
verses.translation: Be not afraid of anything. You will do marvellous work. The moment you fear, you are nobody. It is fear that is the great cause of misery in the world. It is fear that is the greatest of all superstitions. It is fear that is the cause of our woes, and it is fearlessness that brings heaven even in a moment. Therefore, "Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached."
verses.line: it is fearlessness that brings heaven even in a moment.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Mission of the Vedanta, p. 194
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Mission of the Vedanta', Kumbakonam, February 1897.
verses.translation: Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached. Arise, awake! Awake from this hypnotism of weakness. None is really weak; the soul is infinite, omnipotent, and omniscient. Stand up, assert yourself, proclaim the God within you, do not deny Him!
verses.line: Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Address at the Rameswaram Temple on Real Worship, p. 142
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Address at the Rameswaram temple, January 1897.
verses.translation: This is the gist of all worship — to be pure and to do good to others. He who sees Shiva in the poor, in the weak, and in the diseased, really worships Shiva; and if he sees Shiva only in the image, his worship is but preliminary.
verses.line: This is the gist of all worship — to be pure and to do good to others.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Common Bases of Hinduism, p. 382
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897.
verses.translation: Learn everything that is good from others, but bring it in, and in your own way absorb it; do not become others.
verses.line: Learn everything that is good from others, but bring it in, and in your own way absorb it; do not become others.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Common Bases of Hinduism, p. 382
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897. On learning from others without imitation.
verses.translation: You put the seed in the ground, and give it plenty of earth, and air, and water to feed upon; when the seed grows into the plant and into a gigantic tree, does it become the earth, does it become the air, or does it become the water? It becomes the mighty plant, the mighty tree, after its own nature, having absorbed everything that was given to it. Let that be your position.
verses.line: It becomes the mighty plant, the mighty tree, after its own nature, having absorbed everything that was given to it.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Common Bases of Hinduism, p. 382
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897.
verses.translation: We have indeed many things to learn from others, yea, that man who refuses to learn is already dead.
verses.line: that man who refuses to learn is already dead.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Common Bases of Hinduism, p. 378
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897.
verses.translation: Religion is to be realised, not only heard; it is not in learning some doctrine like a parrot.
verses.line: Religion is to be realised, not only heard; it is not in learning some doctrine like a parrot.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Common Bases of Hinduism, p. 384
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897. Closing appeal to rival groups in the hall.
verses.translation: Let us preach where we all agree and leave the differences to remedy themselves.
verses.line: Let us preach where we all agree and leave the differences to remedy themselves.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: My Plan of Campaign, p. 225
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'My Plan of Campaign', Victoria Hall, Madras, February 1897.
verses.translation: And here is the test of truth — anything that makes you weak physically, intellectually, and spiritually, reject as poison; there is no life in it, it cannot be true. Truth is strengthening.
verses.line: anything that makes you weak physically, intellectually, and spiritually, reject as poison;

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: My Plan of Campaign, p. 208
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'My Plan of Campaign', Madras, February 1897, on friends who turned critics.
verses.translation: We hear so much tall talk in this world, of liberal ideas and sympathy with differences of opinion. That is very good, but as a fact, we find that one sympathises with another only so long as the other believes in everything he has to say, but as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.
verses.line: as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Vedantism, p. 131
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'Vedantism', Jaffna, Ceylon, January 1897.
verses.translation: Whatever you think, that you will be. If you think yourselves weak, weak you will be; if you think yourselves strong, strong you will be;
verses.line: If you think yourselves weak, weak you will be; if you think yourselves strong, strong you will be;

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Vedantism, p. 131
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'Vedantism', Jaffna, Ceylon, January 1897.
verses.translation: Make your children strong from their very childhood; teach them not weakness, nor forms, but make them strong; let them stand on their feet — bold, all-conquering, all-suffering; and first of all, let them learn of the glory of the soul.
verses.line: Make your children strong from their very childhood;
verses.misuse: Strong does not mean hard; elsewhere he says love is the only law of life.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Vedantism, p. 135
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'Vedantism', Jaffna, Ceylon, January 1897. Closing words.
verses.translation: Always first learn to be a servant, and then you will be fit to be a master.
verses.line: Always first learn to be a servant, and then you will be fit to be a master.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Vedanta, p. 430
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Vedanta', Lahore, 12 November 1897, telling Indians what he found abroad.
verses.translation: I should be the most ungrateful man if I did not tell you how wonderfully and how hospitably I was received in every country in the West.
verses.line: how wonderfully and how hospitably I was received in every country in the West.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures and Discourses: The Free Soul, p. 12
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Free Soul', New York, 1896.
verses.translation: Therefore, dare to be free, dare to go as far as your thought leads, and dare to carry that out in your life.
verses.line: dare to be free, dare to go as far as your thought leads, and dare to carry that out in your life.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: What We Believe in, p. 358
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from Chicago, 3 March 1894, setting out 'what we believe in'.
verses.translation:
Education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man.
Religion is the manifestation of the Divinity already in man.
verses.line: Education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: Our Duty to the Masses, p. 363
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from Chicago, 23 June 1894, urging the Maharaja to educate the poor.
verses.translation: this life is short, the vanities of the world are transient, but they alone live who live for others, the rest are more dead than alive.
verses.line: they alone live who live for others, the rest are more dead than alive.
verses.misuse: Living for others includes caring for yourself; it is not a call to burn out.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: To My Brave Boys, p. 369
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Alasinga Perumal and the Madras group
verses.setting: Letter 'To my brave boys', New York, 19 November 1894.
verses.translation: Be the servant while leading. Be unselfish, and never listen to one friend in private accusing another. Have infinite patience, and success is yours.
verses.line: Be the servant while leading. Be unselfish, and never listen to one friend in private accusing another. Have infinite patience, and success is yours.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: To My Brave Boys, p. 367
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Alasinga Perumal and the Madras group
verses.setting: Letter 'To my brave boys', New York, 19 November 1894.
verses.translation: Wait, money does not pay, nor name; fame does not pay, nor learning. It is love that pays; it is character that cleaves its way through adamantine walls of difficulties.
verses.line: It is love that pays; it is character that cleaves its way

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: To My Brave Boys, p. 367
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Alasinga Perumal and the Madras group
verses.setting: Letter 'To my brave boys', New York, 19 November 1894.
verses.translation: Struggle, struggle, was my motto for the last ten years. Struggle, still say I. When it was all dark, I used to say, struggle; when light is breaking in, I still say, struggle.
verses.line: When it was all dark, I used to say, struggle; when light is breaking in, I still say, struggle.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Addresses on Bhakti-Yoga: The Preparation, p. 10
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Addresses on Bhakti-Yoga, 'The Preparation'.
verses.translation: The more we come out and do good to others, the more our hearts will be purified, and God will be in them.
verses.line: The more we come out and do good to others, the more our hearts will be purified, and God will be in them.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems: Hold on Yet a While, Brave Heart, pp. 389–390
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Poem 'Hold On Yet a While, Brave Heart', written to the Maharaja of Khetri.
verses.translation: If the sun by the cloud is hidden a bit, If the welkin shows but gloom, Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come. … Not a work will be lost, no struggle vain, Though hopes be blighted, powers gone; … Then hold on yet a while, brave soul, No good is e'er undone.
verses.line: Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems: Hold on Yet a While, Brave Heart, p. 390
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Poem 'Hold On Yet a While, Brave Heart', second stanza.
verses.translation: No winter was but summer came behind, Each hollow crests the wave, They push each other in light and shade; Be steady then and brave.
verses.line: No winter was but summer came behind,

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems: Peace, p. 396
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Poem 'Peace', composed at Ridgely Manor, New York, 1899.
verses.translation: It is sweet rest in music; And pause in sacred art; The silence between speaking; Between two fits of passion — It is the calm of heart.
verses.line: The silence between speaking; Between two fits of passion — It is the calm of heart.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems: The Song of the Sannyâsin, p. 394
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Song of the Sannyasin', written at Thousand Island Park, New York, 1895.
verses.translation: Let one put garlands on, another kick This frame; say naught. No praise or blame can be Where praiser praised, and blamer blamed are one. Thus be thou calm,
verses.line: No praise or blame can be Where praiser praised, and blamer blamed are one.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems: Requiescat in Pace, p. 389
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Poem in memory of his stenographer and friend J. J. Goodwin, August 1898.
verses.translation:
Speed forth, O Soul! upon thy star-strewn path; Speed, blissful one! where thought is ever free, Where time and space no longer mist the view, Eternal peace and blessings be with thee!
Thy service true, complete thy sacrifice, Thy home the heart of love transcendent find; Remembrance sweet, that kills all space and time, Like altar roses fill thy place behind!
verses.line: Remembrance sweet, that kills all space and time, Like altar roses fill thy place behind!

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: A Message of Sympathy to a Friend, p. 355
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: D. R. Balaji Rao, after a severe bereavement
verses.setting: Letter of condolence from Bombay, 23 May 1893, to a friend in deep grief.
verses.translation: Waves may roll over the surface and tempest rage, but deep down there is the stratum of infinite calmness, infinite peace, and infinite bliss.
verses.line: deep down there is the stratum of infinite calmness, infinite peace, and infinite bliss.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Writings: Poems: To an Early Violet, p. 170
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Poem 'To an Early Violet', written from New York, 6 January 1896.
verses.translation:
What though if love itself doth fail, Thy fragrance strewed in vain; What though if bad o'er good prevail, And vice o'er virtue reign:
Change not thy nature, gentle bloom, Thou violet, sweet and pure, But ever pour thy sweet perfume Unasked, unstinted, sure!
verses.line: Change not thy nature, gentle bloom, Thou violet, sweet and pure, But ever pour thy sweet perfume Unasked, unstinted, sure!
verses.misuse: Staying kind is not staying put; you can keep your nature and still leave.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Writings: Prose and Poems: The Cup, p. 177
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda (the poem speaks in the Divine's voice)
verses.setting: Poem 'The Cup' (Complete Works, vol. 6, Writings: Prose and Poems).
verses.translation: This is your task. It has no joy nor grace, But it is not meant for any other hand, And in My universe hath measured place, Take it. I do not bid you understand. I bid you close your eyes to see My face.
verses.line: it is not meant for any other hand,
verses.misuse: Accepting your path is not accepting abuse or injustice; act where you can.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, VII, p. 30
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from Chicago, 24 January 1894, four months after the Parliament.
verses.translation: Have faith in yourselves, great convictions are the mothers of great deeds.
verses.line: Have faith in yourselves, great convictions are the mothers of great deeds.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, XXI, p. 52
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from Washington, 27 October 1894, to his chief disciple in Madras.
verses.translation: Even idiots may stand up to hear themselves praised, and cowards assume the attitude of the brave when everything is sure to turn out well, but the true hero works in silence.
verses.line: cowards assume the attitude of the brave when everything is sure to turn out well, but the true hero works in silence.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, XLVII, p. 91
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from the USA, 9 July 1895, on opposition to his work in America.
verses.translation: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance. Each man who thinks ahead of his time is sure to be misunderstood.
verses.line: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, LXI, p. 108
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Dr. Nanjunda Rao, starting a magazine in Madras
verses.setting: Letter from New York, 14 April 1896, the day before sailing for England.
verses.translation: Go on bravely. Do not expect success in a day or a year. Always hold on to the highest. Be steady. Avoid jealousy and selfishness.
verses.line: Do not expect success in a day or a year.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, LI, p. 281
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from the USA, 30 November 1894, to a young man eager to renounce and serve.
verses.translation: Nothing shall be done in haste. Purity, patience, and perseverance are the three essentials to success and, above all, love. All time is yours, there is no indecent haste.
verses.line: Purity, patience, and perseverance are the three essentials to success and, above all, love.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, CXLVIII, p. 419
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from Ridgely Manor, New York, 1 November 1899, to a disciple in low spirits.
verses.translation: It seems there is a gloom over your mind. Never mind, nothing is to last for ever.
verses.line: Never mind, nothing is to last for ever.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, CLV, p. 429
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from San Francisco, 4 March 1900, written while worn out by work.
verses.translation: By being nervous and fearful we injure others, by being so fearful to hurt we hurt more. By trying so much to avoid evil we fall into its jaws.
verses.line: by being so fearful to hurt we hurt more.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, CLVIII, p. 432
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from Alameda, California, 18 April 1900, after laying down his role as leader.
verses.translation: I am glad I was born, glad I suffered so, glad I did make big blunders, glad to enter peace.
verses.line: I am glad I was born, glad I suffered so, glad I did make big blunders, glad to enter peace.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, CLVIII, p. 432
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from Alameda, 18 April 1900: an honest look back at his own motives.
verses.translation: Behind my work was ambition, behind my love was personality, behind my purity was fear, behind my guidance the thirst of power! Now they are vanishing, and I drift.
verses.line: Behind my work was ambition, behind my love was personality,

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, XCIX, p. 363
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from London, 5 June 1896, about his younger brother Mohin's future in America.
verses.translation: Even if he fails in life, still I will have the satisfaction that he strove to become great and really useful to his country. … I want him to be daring, bold, and to struggle to cut a new path for himself and his nation.
verses.line: Even if he fails in life, still I will have the satisfaction that he strove to become great

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLXV, p. 505
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from San Francisco, 28 March 1900.
verses.translation: Be brave and face everything — come good, come evil, both welcome, both of you my play.
verses.line: Be brave and face everything — come good, come evil, both welcome,

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Lectures and Discourses: Concentration and Breathing, p. 39
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Class talk 'Concentration and Breathing', America (notes in CW 6).
verses.translation: To me the very essence of education is concentration of mind, not the collecting of facts. If I had to do my education over again, and had any voice in the matter, I would not study facts at all. I would develop the power of concentration and detachment, and then with a perfect instrument I could collect facts at will.
verses.line: To me the very essence of education is concentration of mind, not the collecting of facts.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Lectures and Discourses: Concentration and Breathing, p. 38
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Class talk 'Concentration and Breathing', America (notes in CW 6).
verses.translation: Almost all our suffering is caused by our not having the power of detachment.
verses.line: Almost all our suffering is caused by our not having the power of detachment.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures: On Raja-yoga, p. 89
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Notes of a class talk 'On Raja-Yoga' (CW 6).
verses.translation: Do one thing at a time and while doing it put your whole soul into it to the exclusion of all else.
verses.line: Do one thing at a time and while doing it put your whole soul into it to the exclusion of all else.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Inspired Talks, WEDNESDAY, June 26, 1895., p. 14
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Thousand Island Park, New York, 26 June 1895, notes by S. E. Waldo.
verses.translation: We are what our thoughts have made us; so take care of what you think. Words are secondary. Thoughts live, they travel far.
verses.line: We are what our thoughts have made us; so take care of what you think.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Inspired Talks, TUESDAY, June 25, 1895., p. 14
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Thousand Island Park, 25 June 1895, notes by S. E. Waldo.
verses.translation: Neither seek nor avoid, take what comes. It is liberty to be affected by nothing; do not merely endure, be unattached.
verses.line: Neither seek nor avoid, take what comes.
verses.misuse: Not passivity about problems you can fix; it is about not clutching or fleeing.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Discourses on Jnana-Yoga: Jnana Yoga - IV, p. 15
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Class notes 'Jnana-Yoga IV', America, recorded by S. E. Waldo.
verses.translation: "Comfort" is no test of truth; on the contrary, truth is often far from being "comfortable"
verses.line: "Comfort" is no test of truth; on the contrary, truth is often far from being "comfortable"

verses.collection: Notes of Class Talks and Lectures
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures: The Religion of Love, p. 223
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Notes of a lecture 'The Religion of Love', London, 16 November 1895.
verses.translation: Deepen your own power of thought and love. Bring your own lotus to blossom: the bees will come of themselves. Believe first in yourself, then in God.
verses.line: Bring your own lotus to blossom: the bees will come of themselves.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Interviews: India and England, p. 197
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Interview 'India and England', London, 1896.
verses.translation: We may call it God, Allah, Jehovah, the Spirit, Love; it is the same unity that animates all life, from its lowest form to its noblest manifestation in man.
verses.line: We may call it God, Allah, Jehovah, the Spirit, Love;

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Lectures and Discourses: The Gita II, p. 459
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Class on the Gita, San Francisco
verses.setting: Class on the Gita, San Francisco, 28 May 1900, recorded in shorthand by Ida Ansell.
verses.translation: Many a time comes when we want to interpret our weakness and cowardice as forgiveness and renunciation. There is no merit in the renunciation of a beggar.
verses.line: Many a time comes when we want to interpret our weakness and cowardice as forgiveness
verses.misuse: Not a push to retaliate; forgiveness chosen from strength is the real thing.

verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: The Real Nature of Man, p. 82
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: 'The Real Nature of Man', lecture in London, 1896.
verses.translation: Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others; and living this little life is death, simply death, and that is why the fear of death comes. The fear of death can only be conquered when man realises that so long as there is one life in this universe, he is living.
verses.line: Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others;

verses.speaker: Sumitra
verses.setting: Ram has just left for the forest; Sumitra comforts his mother, who cannot stop weeping.
verses.sanskrit_display: शयानमनघं रात्रौ पितेवाभिपरिष्वजन्। धर्मघ्नः संस्पृशञ्छीतश्चन्द्रमा ह्लादयिष्यति॥
verses.translation: When the blameless one lies down at night, the cool moon, which takes away the day's heat, will touch him and embrace him like a father, and gladden his heart.
verses.line: Where you can't reach him tonight, the cool moonlight will hold him the way a father would.

verses.speaker: Lakshman
verses.setting: Sita has been taken; Lakshman comforts Ram, reminding him that trouble touches everyone.
verses.sanskrit_display: यौ धर्मों जगतो नेत्रौ यत्र सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितम्। आदित्यचन्द्रौ ग्रहणमभ्युपेतौ महाबलौ॥
verses.translation: Even the mighty Sun and Moon, the two eyes of the world, on whom everything rests, go through eclipses.
verses.line: Even the sun and the moon, which light the whole world, go through eclipses.

verses.speaker: Lakshman
verses.setting: Sita has been taken; Lakshman, the younger brother, gently tries to bring Ram back to himself.
verses.sanskrit_display: बुद्धिश्च ते महाप्राज्ञ देवैरपि दुरन्वया। शोकेनाभिप्रसुप्तं ते ज्ञानं सम्बोधयाम्यहम्॥
verses.translation: Your understanding, wise one, is beyond even the gods' reckoning. Grief has only put your wisdom to sleep, and I am here to wake it.
verses.line: Your wisdom isn't gone. Grief has only put it to sleep for a while.

verses.speaker: Narrator
verses.setting: Sita hears Hanuman speak of Ram: relief that he is alive, pain that he is suffering.
verses.sanskrit_display: सा रामसंकीर्तनवीतशोका रामस्य शोकेन समानशोका। शरन्मुखेनाम्बुदशेषचन्द्रा निशेव वैदेहसुता बभूव ॥
verses.translation: Hearing Ram spoken of, Sita's sorrow lifted; hearing of his sorrow, she grieved as much as he did. She was like an autumn night, the moon rising through the last of the rain clouds.
verses.line: Relief at the news and grief at his pain, both at once: like a moon rising through rain clouds.

verses.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verses.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verses.sanskrit_display: स कुरुष्व महोत्साहां कृपां मयि नरर्षभ। त्वया नाथवती नाथ अनाथा इव दृश्यते॥
verses.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.
verses.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.

verses.speaker: Sita
verses.setting: Hanuman is about to leave Lanka; Sita, who will be alone again, asks him to stay a little.
verses.sanskrit_display: मम चैवाल्पभाग्यायाः सांनिध्यात् तव वानर । अस्य शोकस्य महतो मुहूर्त मोक्षणं भवेत्॥
verses.translation: And for me, so unlucky, your being near, friend, would free me from this great sorrow, even if only for a moment.
verses.line: Stay a little longer. Just having you near lifts this heavy sorrow, even if only for a moment.

verses.speaker: Hanuman
verses.setting: Hanuman's parting words to Sita before he leaps back across the sea to bring Ram.
verses.sanskrit_display: तदाश्वसिहि भद्रं ते भव त्वं कालकाक्षिणी। नचिराद् द्रक्ष्यसे रामं प्रज्वलन्तमिवानलम्॥
verses.translation: So take heart, bless you. Wait for the time to come. Before long you will see Ram, blazing like fire.
verses.line: Take heart. Hold on and wait for the time to turn. It won't be long now.
verses.misuse: Holding on while help is on its way, not passive waiting; Hanuman leaves to bring help.

verses.speaker: Ram
verses.setting: Ram tells his mother he must leave for fourteen years in the forest.
verses.sanskrit_display: शोकः संधार्यतां मातर्हृदये साधु मा शुचः। वनवासादिहैष्यामि पुनः कृत्वा पितुर्वचः॥
verses.translation: Hold your sorrow gently in your heart, mother; do not grieve. Once I have kept my father's word, I will come back here from the forest.
verses.line: Hold your sorrow gently, mother. I will keep my word, and I will come home to you.

verses.speaker: Shatrughna
verses.setting: After twelve years ruling a distant city, Shatrughna comes home and begs not to be sent far away again.
verses.sanskrit_display: स मे प्रसादं काकुत्स्थ कुरुष्वामितविक्रम। मातृहीनो यथा वत्सो न चिरं प्रवसाम्यहम्॥
verses.translation: Be kind to me, Ram of boundless strength. I cannot go on living far away like a calf without its mother.
verses.line: I can't go on living so far from you, like a calf that has lost its mother.

verses.speaker: Ram
verses.setting: Shatrughna, homesick after twelve years away, has asked to stay; Ram embraces him and answers.
verses.sanskrit_display: ममापि त्वं सुदयितः प्राणैरपि न संशयः। अवश्यं करणीयं च राज्यस्य परिपालनम्॥ तस्मात्त्वं वस काकुत्स्थ सप्तरात्रं मया सह। ऊवं गन्तासि मधुरां सभृत्यबलवाहनः॥
verses.translation: You are dearer to me than life itself, without doubt. But a kingdom must be looked after. So stay with me seven nights, and then go back to Madhura with your people.
verses.line: You are dearer to me than my own life. Stay with me a while before you go back.

verses.speaker: Kausalya
verses.setting: Holding back tears, Kausalya blesses her son before he leaves for fourteen years in the forest.
verses.sanskrit_display: यं पालयसि धर्म त्वं प्रीत्या च नियमेन च। स वै राघवशार्दूल धर्मस्त्वामभिरक्षतु॥
verses.translation: May the goodness you have kept so gladly and so faithfully protect you, tiger of the Raghus.
verses.line: May the good you have lived by, gladly and faithfully, now protect you.
verses.misuse: A mother's blessing, not a promise that good people never suffer.

verses.collection: Manas: Sundar Kand, Refuge of Vibhishan
verses.speaker: Ram
verses.setting: Ravana's brother Vibhishan has come asking for shelter; Sugriva suspects a spy, and Ram answers.
verses.sanskrit_display: कोटि बिप्र बध लागहिं जाहू। आएँ सरन तजउँ नहिं ताहू॥ सनमुख होइ जीव मोहि जबहीं। जन्म कोटि अघ नासहिं तबहीं ॥
verses.translation: Even someone who carries the sin of killing countless brahmins, if he comes to me for shelter, I will not turn away. The moment a soul turns to face me, the wrongs of countless lives are wiped away.
verses.line: I never turn away anyone who comes to me. The moment you turn toward me, your past is washed away.
verses.misuse: Not a licence to keep doing harm; the turning has to be real.

verses.collection: Manas: Sundar Kand, Refuge of Vibhishan
verses.speaker: Ram
verses.setting: Sugriva fears Vibhishan is a spy; Ram says it makes no difference.
verses.sanskrit_display: जग महुँ सखा निसाचर जेते। लछिमनु हनइ निमिष महुँ तेते॥ जौं सभीत आवा सरनाईं। रखिहउँ ताहि प्रान की नाईं ॥
verses.translation: Friend, Lakshman could destroy every demon in the world in a moment. And if he has come to me in fear, seeking shelter, I will keep him as dear as my own life.
verses.line: If someone comes to me afraid, looking for shelter, I will keep them as dear as my own life.

verses.collection: Manas: Sundar Kand, Refuge of Vibhishan
verses.speaker: Vibhishan
verses.setting: Vibhishan, newly welcomed by Ram, can hardly believe it.
verses.sanskrit_display: मैं निसिचर अति अधम सुभाऊ। सुभ आचरनु कीन्ह नहिं काऊ॥ जासु रूप मुनि ध्यान न आवा। तेहिं प्रभु हरषि हृदयँ मोहि लावा ॥
verses.translation: I am a demon, low by nature; I have never done a single good deed. And yet the Lord whose form sages cannot reach even in meditation has gladly held me to his heart.
verses.line: I had never done anything good, and still he was glad to hold me to his heart.
verses.misuse: Vibhishan's self-judgement is harsh; the point is the welcome, not the self-contempt.

verses.collection: Manas: Sundar Kand, Hanuman reaches Sita
verses.speaker: Hanuman
verses.setting: Alone in Ravana's garden, Sita has just cried 'He has forgotten me completely'; Hanuman answers.
verses.sanskrit_display: मातु कुसल प्रभु अनुज समेता। तव दुख दुखी सुकृपा निकेता॥ जनि जननी मानह जियँ ऊना। तुम्ह ते प्रेमु राम कें दूना ॥
verses.translation: Mother, the Lord and his brother are well, but your sorrow makes him sorrowful. Don't let your heart feel small, mother: Ram's love for you is twice yours.
verses.line: Don't think you've been forgotten. He hurts because you hurt, and his love for you is twice yours.

verses.collection: Manas: Uttar Kand, Ram comes home
verses.speaker: Bharat
verses.setting: After fourteen years apart, Ram embraces Bharat and asks how he is; Bharat can barely speak.
verses.sanskrit_display: बूझत कृपानिधि कुसल भरतहि बचन बेगि न आवई॥ सुनु सिवा सो सुख बचन मन ते भिन्न जान जो पावई॥ अब कुसल कौसलनाथ आरत जानि जन दरसन दियो। बूड़त बिरह बारीस कृपानिधान मोहि कर गहि लियो ॥
verses.translation: When the Lord asked Bharat how he was, no words would come. Shiva says: Parvati, that joy is beyond words and thought; only one who has felt it knows. Bharat said: Now I am well, Lord of Kosala. You saw how I suffered and showed yourself to me. I was drowning in the sea of separation, and you took me by the hand.
verses.line: I was drowning in missing you, and you took me by the hand.

verses.collection: Manas: Uttar Kand, Ram comes home
verses.speaker: Narrator
verses.setting: Ram returns to Ayodhya after fourteen years; his mothers run to meet him.
verses.sanskrit_display: जनु धेनु बालक बच्छ तजि गृहँ चरन बन परबस गईं। दिन अंत पुर रुख स्रवत थन हुंकार करि धावत भईं॥ अति प्रेम प्रभु सब मातु भेटीं बचन मृदु बहुबिधि कहे। गइ बिषम बिपति बियोगभव तिन्ह हरष सुख अगनित लहे॥
verses.translation: Like cows that had to leave their young calves at home to graze in the forest, and at day's end run lowing toward the village, milk flowing, so the mothers ran. With great love the Lord met each of them and spoke many gentle words. The hard pain of separation left them, and they found countless joys.
verses.line: Like cows running home at dusk to their calves, the mothers ran to hold their sons again.

verses.collection: Manas: Ayodhya Kand, Chitrakoot: Ram to Bharat
verses.speaker: Ram
verses.setting: Bharat blames himself for his mother's scheme; Ram answers him in front of the elders.
verses.sanskrit_display: करम बचन मानस बिमल तुम्ह समान तुम्ह तात। गुर समाज लघु बंधु गुन कुसमयँ किमि कहि जात ॥
verses.translation: Brother, in deed, word and mind you are spotless; the only one like you is you. But how can I praise a younger brother's goodness in front of our elders, at a hard time like this?
verses.line: In what you do, say and think, you are clean. There is no one like you.

verses.collection: Manas: Ayodhya Kand, Vasishtha counsels Bharat
verses.speaker: Narrator
verses.setting: After the king's funeral, the royal guru Vasishtha gathers the court to counsel the grieving Bharat.
verses.sanskrit_display: कहत राम गुन सील सुभाऊ। सजल नयन पुलकेउ मुनिराऊ॥ बहुरि लखन सिय प्रीति बखानी। सोक सनेह मगन मुनि ग्यानी ॥
verses.translation: As he spoke of Ram's goodness, gentleness and nature, the great sage's eyes filled with tears and he trembled. Then, praising the love of Lakshman and Sita, the wise sage was lost in sorrow and affection.
verses.line: Even the wise old teacher's eyes filled with tears as he spoke of the ones he loved.

verses.collection: Manas: Ayodhya Kand, Kausalya lets her son go
verses.speaker: Kausalya
verses.setting: Kausalya blesses Ram as he leaves for fourteen years in the forest.
verses.sanskrit_display: देव पितर सब तुम्हहि गोसाईं। राखहुँ पलक नयन की नाईं॥ अवधि अंबु प्रिय परिजन मीना। तुम्ह करुनाकर धरम धुरीना ॥
verses.translation: May all the gods and ancestors guard you, my lord, the way eyelids guard the eyes. The term of your exile is the water, and your loved ones are the fish in it; you are kind and steadfast in what is right.
verses.line: May you be guarded the way eyelids guard the eyes.

verses.collection: Manas: Kishkindha Kand, Hanuman meets Ram
verses.speaker: Ram
verses.setting: Hanuman, ashamed that he did not recognise Ram at first, falls weeping at his feet.
verses.sanskrit_display: सुनु कपि जियँ मानसि जनि ऊना। तैं मम प्रिय लछिमन ते दूना॥ समदरसी मोहि कह सब कोऊ। सेवक प्रिय अनन्य गति सोऊ ॥
verses.translation: Listen, Hanuman: don't let your heart feel small. You are twice as dear to me as Lakshman. Everyone calls me impartial, yet the one who serves me is dear to me, because he has no other refuge.
verses.line: Don't feel small. You are twice as dear to me as my own brother.

verses.speaker: Sugriva
verses.setting: Sugriva has just given Ram the scarf Sita dropped; Ram is weeping.
verses.sanskrit_display: कह सुग्रीव सुनहु रघुबीरा। तजहु सोच मन आनहु धीरा॥ सब प्रकार करिहउँ सेवकाई। जेहि बिधि मिलिहि जानकी आई ॥
verses.translation: Sugriva said: Listen, Raghuvir. Put aside your worry and steady your heart. I will serve you in every way, whatever it takes for Janaki to come back to you.
verses.line: Put down your worry and steady your heart. I'll help you in every way I can.

verses.collection: Manas: Ayodhya Kand, The family council at Chitrakoot
verses.speaker: Bharat
verses.setting: Bharat, in front of the council, speaks of how Ram treats those who come to him.
verses.sanskrit_display: तेउ सुनि सरन सामुहें आए। सकृत प्रनामु किहें अपनाए॥ देखि दोष कबहुँ न उर आने। सुनि गुन साधु समाज बखाने ॥
verses.translation: Even such people, hearing of you, came before you for shelter, and with a single bow you made them your own. You saw their faults but never kept them in your heart; you heard their virtues and praised them among the good.
verses.line: Come once, bow once, and you are taken in. Your faults are seen, but never held against you.

verses.speaker: Vyasa
verses.setting: Late in the forest exile, Vyasa visits the Pandavas and comforts the despondent Yudhishthira.
verses.sanskrit_display: सुखस्यानन्तरं दुःखं दुःखस्यानन्तरं सुखम् / पर्यायेणोपसर्पन्ते नरं नेमिमरा इव
verses.translation: After happiness comes sorrow, and after sorrow, happiness. They come round to a person in turn, like the spokes of a wheel to the rim.
verses.line: After sorrow, happiness comes round again, the way each spoke of a wheel comes back to the top.

verses.speaker: Krishna
verses.setting: Arjuna asks which way of devotion is best; Krishna promises what he does for those who turn to him.
verses.sanskrit_display: तेषामहं समुद्धर्ता मृत्युसंसारसागरात् । भवामि नचिरात्पार्थ मय्यावेशितचेतसाम् ॥
verses.translation: For those whose minds are absorbed in me, O Partha, I very soon become the one who lifts them out of the ocean of death and endless change.
verses.line: Whoever rests their heart in me, I lift out of the drowning sea, and soon.

verses.speaker: Vishvamitra
verses.setting: Vishvamitra gently invites the withdrawn Rama to speak.
verses.sanskrit_display: यथाभिमतमाशु त्वं ब्रूहि प्राप्स्यसि चानघ । सर्वमेव पुनर्येन भेत्स्यन्ते त्वां तु नाधयः ॥
verses.translation: Say quickly whatever you wish, blameless one, and you will have it, by which these sorrows will never pierce you again.
verses.line: Say freely what is on your heart, blameless one. These sorrows need not keep wounding you.

verses.speaker: Vasishtha
verses.setting: Queen Lila is shattered by her husband's death; the goddess Sarasvati sees her.
verses.sanskrit_display: अथ तामतिमात्रविह्वलां सकृपाकाशभवा सरस्वती । शफरीं ह्रदशोषविह्वलां प्रथमा वृष्टिरिवान्वकम्पत ॥
verses.translation: Then Sarasvati, born of the sky, was moved with pity for her, utterly overwhelmed, as the first rain pities a little fish gasping in a drying pond.
verses.line: Seeing her undone by grief, the goddess was moved, like first rain reaching a fish in a drying pond.

verses.speaker: Prahlada
verses.setting: King Prahlada, after long inner work and heavy rule, speaks to Vishnu.
verses.sanskrit_display: हिताहितविचारेण राजकार्यशतेन च । अत्यहं श्रमितो देव क्षणं विश्रामतां गतः ॥
verses.translation: Weighing what helps and what harms, and with hundreds of royal duties, I was utterly worn out, Lord. For a moment now, I have found rest.
verses.line: So many decisions, so many duties, I was utterly worn out. For a moment now, I've found rest.

verses.speaker: Vasishtha
verses.setting: After the story of King Suraghu, Vasishtha describes the relief of seeing clearly.
verses.sanskrit_display: एतां दृष्टिमवष्टभ्य न मनः परितप्यते । घोरे तमसि निर्मग्नं लब्धदीपं शिशुर्यथा ॥
verses.translation: Holding to this way of seeing, the mind no longer burns with distress, like a child sunk in pitch darkness who has been given a lamp.
verses.line: Seeing this way, the mind stops burning, like a child lost in the dark who is handed a lamp.

verses.speaker: Vasishtha
verses.setting: Vasishtha tells Rama where a tired person can rest.
verses.sanskrit_display: स्निग्धशीतवचःपत्रे सच्छाये स्मितपुष्पके । क्षणाद्विश्रम्यते राम भृशं सुजनचम्पके ॥
verses.translation: Under the champak tree of a good person, whose leaves are tender, cooling words, with good shade and smiles for flowers, one rests at once, Rama, and deeply.
verses.line: A kind person is a shady tree: cool words for leaves, smiles for flowers. Rest there a while.

verses.collection: Yoga Vasishtha: The tree of wisdom
verses.speaker: Vasishtha
verses.setting: Vasishtha describes the cool shade of the tree of understanding.
verses.sanskrit_display: यस्यामवान्तरश्रान्तो विश्राम्यति मनोमृगः । आजन्मजीर्णपथिकः पथि कोलाहलाकुलः ॥
verses.translation: In its shade the deer of the mind, tired out along the way, rests: a traveller worn out since birth on a road full of noise.
verses.line: In its shade the tired deer of the mind rests, like a traveller worn out by a long, noisy road.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 492
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 492
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Mary Hale, whose father had just died
verses.setting: Condolence letter from Pasadena, 20 February 1900, on the death of Mary Hale's father.
verses.translation: Your letter bearing the sad news of Mr. Hale's passing away reached me yesterday. I am sorry, because in spite of monastic training, the heart lives on; and then Mr. Hale was one of the best souls I met in life. Of course you are sorry, miserable, and so are Mother Church and Harriet and the rest, especially as this is the first grief of its kind you have met, is it not? I have lost many, suffered much, and the most curious cause of suffering when somebody goes off is the feeling that I was not good enough to that person. When my father died, it was a pang for months, and I had been so disobedient. You have been very dutiful; if you feel anything like that, it is only a form of sorrow.
verses.line: the most curious cause of suffering when somebody goes off is the feeling that I was not good enough to that person.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 492
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 492
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Mary Hale, whose father had just died
verses.setting: A monk's condolence letter, 20 February 1900: he admits his own sorrow at the death of a friend.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 493
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 493
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Mary Hale, in her first great grief
verses.setting: Condolence letter, 20 February 1900, to a friend meeting her first bereavement.
verses.translation: Just now I am afraid life begins for you, Mary, in earnest. We may read books, hear lectures, and talk miles, but experience is the one teacher, the one eye-opener. It is best as it is. We learn, through smiles and tears we learn. We don't know why, but we see it is so; and that is enough. Of course Mother Church has the solace of her religion. I wish we could all dream undisturbed good dreams.
verses.line: We learn, through smiles and tears we learn. We don't know why, but we see it is so; and that is enough.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 493
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 493
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Mary Hale, whose father had just died
verses.setting: Condolence letter, 20 February 1900: a friend who has known many losses offers to carry hers.
verses.translation: You have had shelter all your life. I was in the glare, burning and panting all the time. Now for a moment you have caught a glimpse of the other side. My life is made up of continuous blows like that, and hundred times worse, because of poverty, treachery, and my own foolishness! Pessimism! You will understand it, how it comes. Well, well, what shall I say to you, Mary? You know all the talks; only I say this and it is true — if it were possible to exchange grief, and had I a cheerful mind, I would exchange mine for your grief ever and always. Mother knows best.
verses.line: if it were possible to exchange grief, and had I a cheerful mind, I would exchange mine for your grief ever and always.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, XXXI, p. 70
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, XXXI, p. 70
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Sara Ole Bull ('Dhira Mata'), on the death of her father
verses.setting: Condolence letter, 20 January 1895, on where the departed are.
verses.translation: Each soul is a star, and all stars are set in that infinite azure, that eternal sky, the Lord. There is the root, the reality, the real individuality of each and all. Religion began with the search after some of these stars that had passed beyond our horizon, and ended in finding them all in God, and ourselves in the same place. The whole secret is, then, that your father has given up the old garment he was wearing and is standing where he was through all eternity. Will he manifest another such garment in this or any other world? I sincerely pray that he may not, until he does so in full consciousness. I pray that none may be dragged anywhither by the unseen power of his own past actions. I pray that all may be free, that is to say, may know that they are free. And if they are to dream again, let us pray that their dreams be all of peace and bliss. . . .
verses.line: Each soul is a star, and all stars are set in that infinite azure, that eternal sky, the Lord.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, XXXV, p. 500
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, XXXV, p. 500
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Prof. John Henry Wright, whose 16-year-old daughter had died
verses.setting: Condolence letter from London, 16 May 1896, to the professor who sent him to Chicago.
verses.translation: This is the world my brother — this illusion of Mâyâ — the Lord alone is true. The forms are evanescent; but the spirit, being in the Lord and of the Lord, is immortal and omnipresent. All that we ever had are round us this minute, for the spirit can neither come nor go, it only changes its plane of manifestation.
verses.line: All that we ever had are round us this minute, for the spirit can neither come nor go, it only changes its plane of manifestation.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: A Message Of Sympathy To A Friend, p. 355
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: A Message Of Sympathy To A Friend, p. 355
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: D. R. Balaji Rao, who had lost his son
verses.setting: Condolence letter from Bombay, 23 May 1893: a prayer admitting the heart's fight against acceptance.
verses.translation: Blessed be Thy name, O Lord! And Thy will be done. Lord, we know that we are to submit; Lord, we know that it is the Mother's hand that is striking, and "The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak." There is, Father of Love, an agony at the heart which is fighting against that calm resignation which Thou teachest". Give us strength, O Thou who sawest Thy whole family destroyed before Thine eyes, with Thine hands crossed on Thy breast. Come, Lord, Thou Great Teacher, who has taught us that the soldier is only to obey and speak not. Come, Lord, come Arjuna's Charioteer, and teach me as Thou once taughtest him, that resignation in Thyself is the highest end and aim of this life, so that with those great ones of old, I may also firmly and resignedly cry, Om Shri Krishnârpanamastu.
verses.line: There is, Father of Love, an agony at the heart which is fighting against that calm resignation which Thou teachest

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Writings: Poems: Light, p. 168
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Writings: Poems: Light, p. 168
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Four lines from a letter of 26 December 1900, written days after a close friend, Captain Sevier, died.
verses.translation: I look behind and after And find that all is right, In my deepest sorrows There is a soul of light.
verses.line: I look behind and after And find that all is right, In my deepest sorrows There is a soul of light.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, XXIII, p. 316
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, XXIII, p. 316
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter to the Hale sisters, autumn 1894, weeping with relief after news from India.
verses.translation: Glory unto Jagadambâ (Mother of the Universe)! I have gained beyond expectations. The prophet has been honoured and with a vengeance. I am weeping like a child at His mercy — He never leaves His servant, sisters. The letter I send you will explain all, and the printed things are coming to the American people. The names there are the very flower of our country. The President was the chief nobleman of Calcutta, and the other man Mahesh Chandra Nyâyaratna is the principal of the Sanskrit College and the chief Brahmin in all India and recognised by the Government as such. The letter will tell you all. O sisters! What a rogue am I that in the face of such mercies sometimes the faith totters — seeing every moment that I am in His hands. Still the mind sometimes gets despondent. Sister, there is a God — a Father — a Mother who never leaves His Children, never, never, never. Put uncanny theories aside and becoming children take refuge in Him. I cannot write more — I am weeping like a woman.
verses.line: Sister, there is a God — a Father — a Mother who never leaves His Children, never, never, never.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, XXIII, p. 316
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, XXIII, p. 316
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, LXII, p. 304
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, LXII, p. 304
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Sara Bull (letter), addressed as a prayer to God
verses.setting: Letter from New York, 11 April 1895, alone and struggling in a foreign country.
verses.translation: Truce to this "right sort of presentation". Thou art my right, Thou my wrong, my Shiva. Lord, since a child I have taken refuge in Thee. Thou wilt be with me in the tropics or at the poles, on the tops of mountains or in the depth of oceans. My stay — my guide in life — my refuge — my friend — my teacher — my God — my real Self, Thou wilt never leave me, never. I know it for sure. Sometimes I become weak, being alone and struggling against odds, my God; and I think of human help. Save Thou me for ever from these weaknesses, and may I never, never seek for help from any being but Thee. If a man puts his trust in another good man, he is never betrayed, never forsaken. Wilt Thou forsake me, Father of all good, Thou who knowest that all my life I am Thy servant and Thine alone? Wilt Thou give me over to be played upon by others, or dragged down by evil? He will never leave me, I am sure, mother.
verses.line: Thou wilt be with me in the tropics or at the poles, on the tops of mountains or in the depth of oceans.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, IX, p. 452
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, IX, p. 452
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Prof. John Henry Wright (poem sent in a letter)
verses.setting: Poem in a letter from Salem, 4 September 1893, just before the Parliament of Religions.
verses.translation: Meseems I hear Thee whispering sweet My love, "I am near", "I am near". My heart gets strong. With Thee, my love, A thousand deaths no fear. Thou speakest in the mother's lay That shuts the baby's eye; When innocent children laugh and play I see Thee standing by.
verses.line: Meseems I hear Thee whispering sweet My love, "I am near", "I am near". My heart gets strong.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures: On Bhakti-Yoga, p. 91
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures: On Bhakti-Yoga, p. 91
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: A prayer he gave students in his notes on Bhakti-Yoga.
verses.translation: Pray, "I do not want wealth or beauty, this world or another, but Thee, O God! Lord! I have become weary. Oh, take me by the hand, Lord, I take shelter with Thee Make me Thy servant. Be Thou my refuge."
verses.line: Lord! I have become weary. Oh, take me by the hand, Lord, I take shelter with Thee

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CXXIV, p. 448
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CXXIV, p. 448
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from Belur, March 1898, to brother monks running a new centre.
verses.translation: Do look after Alasinga. I have an idea that he is breaking himself with work. Tell him, the best work is only done by alternate repose and work. Give him all my love. We had two public lectures in Calcutta, one from Miss Noble and the other from our Sharat. Both of them did very well indeed; there was great enthusiasm, which shows that the Calcutta public has not forgotten us. Some of the members of the Math had a touch of influenza. They are all right now. The thing is working nicely. Shri (Holy) Mother is here, and the European and American ladies went the other day to see her, and what do you think, Mother ate with them even there! Is not that grand? The Lord is watching over us; there is no fear; do not lose your nerves, keep your health and take things easy. It is always good to give a few strong strokes and rest on your oars. Rakhal is living with the new land and buildings. I was not satisfied with the Mahotsava this year. What it should be is a grand mixture of all the different phases here. We shall try it next year — I shall send instructions. With love to all of you there and blessings.
verses.line: The Lord is watching over us; there is no fear; do not lose your nerves, keep your health and take things easy.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, LII, p. 525
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, LII, p. 525
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.listener: Mrs. Blodgett ('Aunt Roxy'), his hostess in Los Angeles
verses.setting: Letter of 2 May 1900, in failing health, near the end of his second American tour.
verses.translation: Well, dear good mother, may all blessings attend you and peace. I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me. With love to Kate,
verses.line: I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, CIII, p. 160
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, CIII, p. 160
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from Belur, 18 May 1901, ill and grieving the sudden death of the Raja of Khetri.
verses.translation: The Raja of Khetri died from a fall a few months ago. So you see things are all gloomy with me just now, and my own health is wretched. Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.
verses.line: Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVII, p. 494
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVII, p. 494
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Letter from San Francisco, 2 March 1900, after two very hard years.
verses.translation: How are you all? Give Mother my heartfelt love. I wish I had her strength, she is a true Christian. My health is much better, but the old strength is not there yet. I hope it will come some day, but then, one had to work so hard to do the least little thing. I wish I had rest and peace for a few days at least, which I am sure I can get with the sisters at Chicago. Well, Mother knows best, as I say always. She knows best. The last two years have been specially bad. I have been living in mental hell. It is partially lifted now, and I hope for better days, better states. All blessings on you and the sisters and Mother. Mary, you have been always the sweetest notes in my jarring and clashing life. Then you had the great good Karma to start without oppressive surroundings. I never know a moment's peaceful life. It has always been high pressure, mentally. Lord bless you.
verses.line: I have been living in mental hell. It is partially lifted now, and I hope for better days, better states.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Hints On Practical Spirituality, p. 36
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Hints On Practical Spirituality, p. 36
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Lecture 'Hints on Practical Spirituality', just before quoting Gita 6.40.
verses.translation: But though it is so hard to reach the goal, yet even our smallest attempts are not in vain. We know that nothing is lost. In the Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna, "Those who fail in attaining perfection in Yoga in this life, are they destroyed like the clouds of summer?" Krishna replies, "Nothing, my friend, is lost in this world. Whatever one does, that remains as one's own, and if the fruition of Yoga does not come in this life, one takes it up again in the next birth." Otherwise, how do you explain the marvellous childhood of Jesus, Buddha, Shankara?
verses.line: But though it is so hard to reach the goal, yet even our smallest attempts are not in vain. We know that nothing is lost.

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: Maya And Freedom, p. 123
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: Maya And Freedom, p. 123
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Lecture 'Maya and Freedom', London, 22 October 1896.
verses.translation: Is there no hope then? True it is that we are all slaves of Maya, born in Maya, and live in Maya. Is there then no way out, no hope? That we are all miserable, that this world is really a prison, that even our so-called trailing beauty is but a prison-house, and that even our intellects and minds are prison-houses, have been known for ages upon ages. There has never been a man, there has never been a human soul, who has not felt this sometime or other, however he may talk. And the old people feel it most, because in them is the accumulated experience of a whole life, because they cannot be easily cheated by the lies of nature. Is there no way out? We find that with all this, with this terrible fact before us, in the midst of sorrow and suffering, even in this world where life and death are synonymous, even here, there is a still small voice that is ringing through all ages, through every country, and in every heart: "This My Maya is divine, made up of qualities, and very difficult to cross. Yet those that come unto Me, cross the river of life." "Come unto Me all ye that labour and are heavy laden and I will give you rest." This is the voice that is leading us forward. Man has heard it, and is hearing it all through the ages. This voice comes to men when everything seems to be lost and hope has fled, when man's dependence on his own strength has been crushed down and everything seems to melt away between his fingers, and life is a hopeless ruin. Then he hears it. This is called religion.
verses.line: in the midst of sorrow and suffering, even in this world where life and death are synonymous, even here, there is a still small voice

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Lectures and Discourses: Christ, The Messenger, p. 153
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Lectures and Discourses: Christ, The Messenger, p. 153
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Lecture 'Christ, the Messenger', Los Angeles, 1900.
verses.translation: In a sense you are all Prophets; every one of you is a Prophet, bearing the burden of the world on your own shoulders. Have you ever seen a man, have you ever seen a woman, who is not quietly, patiently, bearing his or her little burden of life? The great Prophets were giants — they bore a gigantic world on their shoulders. Compared with them we are pigmies, no doubt, yet we are doing the same task; in our little circles, in our little homes, we are bearing our little crosses. There is no one so evil, no one so worthless, but he has to bear his own cross. But with all our mistakes, with all our evil thoughts and evil deeds, there is a bright spot somewhere, there is still somewhere the golden thread through which we are always in touch with the divine. For, know for certain, that the moment the touch of the divine is lost there would be annihilation. And because none can be annihilated, there is always somewhere in our heart of hearts, however low and degraded we may be, a little circle of light which is in constant touch with the divine.
verses.line: there is always somewhere in our heart of hearts, however low and degraded we may be, a little circle of light

verses.display_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Lectures and Discourses: Is Vedanta The Future Religion?, p. 127
verses.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Lectures and Discourses: Is Vedanta The Future Religion?, p. 127
verses.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verses.setting: Lecture 'Is Vedanta the Future Religion?', San Francisco, 8 April 1900.
verses.translation: These are what Vedanta has not to give. No book. No man to be singled out from the rest of mankind — "You are worms, and we are the Lord God!" — none of that. If you are the Lord God, I also am the Lord God. So Vedanta knows no sin. There are mistakes but no sin; and in the long run everything is going to be all right. No Satan — none of this nonsense. Vedanta believes in only one sin, only one in the world, and it is this: the moment you think you are a sinner or anybody is a sinner, that is sin. From that follows every other mistake or what is usually called sin. There have been many mistakes in our lives. But we are going on. Glory be unto us that we have made mistakes! Take a long look at your past life. If your present condition is good, it has been caused by all the past mistakes as well as successes. Glory be unto success! Glory be unto mistakes! Do not look back upon what has been done. Go ahead!
verses.line: There are mistakes but no sin; and in the long run everything is going to be all right.

verses.collection: Vinay Patrika: kindness that does not depend on us
verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas, looking back at his failings, on why he was not abandoned.
verses.sanskrit_display: मेरो भलो कियो राम आपनी भलाई। हौं तो साई-द्रोही पै सेवक-हित साई॥ पाथ माथे चढ़े तृन तुलसी ज्यों नीचो। बोरत न बारि ताहि जानि आपु सींचो॥
verses.translation: Ram did me good out of his own goodness. I have wronged my master, yet my master is good to his servant. Tulsi is as low as a blade of grass floating on the water; the water does not drown it, knowing it was the water that made it grow.
verses.line: Water does not drown the grass it once watered. The one who raised you will not let you sink.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.collection: Vinay Patrika: "I have fallen, you lift the fallen"
verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas finds, almost playfully, a reason for hope in his own failings.
verses.sanskrit_display: मैं हरि पतित-पावन सुने। मैं पतित तुम पतित-पावन दोउ बानक बने॥
verses.translation: Hari, I have heard you are the one who lifts the fallen. I am fallen and you lift the fallen: the two of us are a perfect match.
verses.line: I have fallen, and you lift the fallen. We are a perfect match.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas, feeling he has no one to tell, speaks to Ram.
verses.sanskrit_display: कहाँ जाउँ, कासों कहौं, कौन सुने दीनकी। त्रिभुवन तुही गति सब अंगहीनकी॥ जग जगदीस घर धरनि घनेरे हैं। निराधारके अधार गुनगन तेरे हैं॥
verses.translation: Where do I go, whom do I tell, who will listen to someone so low? In all three worlds you alone are the way for the one who has lost every support. The world is full of would-be lords in every house, but your goodness is the support of those who have none.
verses.line: Where do I go, whom do I tell? You are the support of those who have none.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.collection: Vinay Patrika: the burning heart eases
verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas on what finally cools a heart on fire.
verses.sanskrit_display: राम-नामके जपे जाइ जियकी जरनि।
verses.translation: By repeating Ram's name, the burning of the heart goes away.
verses.line: Say his name, and slowly the burning in the heart eases.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.collection: Vinay Patrika: who feels another's pain
verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas on why he brings his sorrow only to Ram.
verses.sanskrit_display: दीनबन्धु दूसरो कहँ पावों ? को तुम बिनु पर-पीर पाइ है? केहि दीनता सुनावों॥
verses.translation: Where would I find another friend of the lowly? Who but you feels another's pain? To whom else would I tell my sorrow?
verses.line: Who else feels another's pain as their own? To whom else would I tell mine?
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.collection: Vinay Patrika: "Tulsi, you are mine. Do not lose heart"
verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Frightened by hard times, Tulsidas asks Ram to say the words he needs to hear.
verses.sanskrit_display: रीति सुनि रावरी प्रतीति-प्रीति रावरे सों, डरत हौं देखि कलिकालको कहरु। कहेही बनैगी कै कहाये, बलि जाउँ, राम, “तुलसी ! तू मेरो, हारि हिये न हहरु'॥
verses.translation: Having heard your ways, my trust and love are in you, yet I am afraid, seeing the cruelty of these times. It will only be well if you say it, or have it said, Ram: "Tulsi, you are mine. Do not lose heart, do not tremble."
verses.line: "You are mine. Do not lose heart, do not tremble."
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.collection: Vinay Patrika: what I could not fix
verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas, after trying and failing to set himself right.
verses.sanskrit_display: मेरी न बने बनाये मेरे कोटि कलप लौं राम! रावरे बनाये बने पल पाउ मैं।
verses.translation: What I try to make of myself would not come right in millions of ages; Ram, what you make comes right in a quarter of a moment.
verses.line: What I could not fix in ages, grace can mend in a moment.
verses.misuse: Not a reason to stop trying; a release from the belief that everything rests on you.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.collection: Vinay Patrika: "Good or bad, your own"
verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas asks to be seen, faults and all.
verses.sanskrit_display: कबहुँ कृपा करि रघुबीर! मोहू चितैहो। भलो-बुरो जन आपनो, जिय जानि दयानिधि ! अवगुन अमित बितैहो॥
verses.translation: Raghubir, will you ever kindly look my way too? Treasury of mercy, knowing in your heart that good or bad I am your own, will you let my countless faults go?
verses.line: Good or bad, I am still your own. Look my way, and let my faults go.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.collection: Vinay Patrika: "Where is there a place for me?"
verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas, weak in body and spirit, looks for a place to rest.
verses.sanskrit_display: जाउँ कहाँ, ठौर है कहाँ देव! दुखित-दीनको ? को कृपालु स्वामी-सारिखो, राखै सरनागत सब अँग बल-बिहीनको ॥
verses.translation: Where do I go? Where is there a place for the hurting and poor, Lord? Who is as kind as my master, who keeps the one who comes for shelter even when every limb has lost its strength?
verses.line: When every limb has lost its strength, there is still a place where you are kept.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas's advice to himself when weighed down.
verses.sanskrit_display: तुलसी राम कृपालु सों कहि सुनाउ गुन दोष। होय दूबरी दीनता परम पीन संतोष॥
verses.translation: Tulsi, tell the kind Ram all of it, your good points and your faults. Your misery will grow thin and your contentment will grow full.
verses.line: Tell the kind one everything, good and bad. The heaviness thins; peace grows.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas on finding no helpers.
verses.sanskrit_display: बाधक सब सब के भए साधक भए न कोइ। तुलसी राम कृपालु तें भलो होइ सो होइ॥
verses.translation: Everyone became an obstacle to everyone; no one became a helper. Tulsi says: whatever good comes will come from the kind Ram.
verses.line: When no one around you helps, good can still come from somewhere kinder.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas recalls the feet that freed Ahalya from her curse.
verses.sanskrit_display: सिला साप मोचन चरन सुमिरहु तुलसीदास । तजहु सोच संकट मिटिहिं पूजहि मनकी आस॥
verses.translation: Tulsidas, remember the feet that freed the woman turned to stone from her curse. Let your worry go: the trouble will pass and the heart's hope will be met.
verses.line: Let the worry go. The trouble will pass; the heart's hope can still be met.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas on his own childhood: abandoned at birth, he grew up begging.
verses.sanskrit_display: मातु-पिताँ जग जाइ तज्यो बिधिहूँ न लिखी कछु भाल भलाई। नीच, निरादरभाजन, कादर, कूकर-टूकन लागि ललाई॥ रामु-सुभाउ सुन्यो तुलसीं प्रभुसों कह्यो बारक पेटु खलाई। स्वारथको परमारथको रघुनाथु सो साहेबु, खोरि न लाई॥
verses.translation: My mother and father brought me into the world and left me; fate wrote nothing good on my forehead. Lowly, scorned, timid, I hungered like a dog for scraps. Then Tulsi heard of Ram's nature and, just once, showed the Lord his empty stomach. Such a master is Raghunath that he held nothing back, in this world or the next.
verses.line: Abandoned as a child, he poured out his hunger just once, and was held.
verses.rights: Poem public domain (medieval). Edition scanned on archive.org (Gita Press); Gita Press Hindi commentary not copied (Poddar d. 1971, still in copyright in India until 2032).

verses.collection: Kavitavali: where no one else is
verses.speaker: Tulsidas
verses.setting: Tulsidas imagines the hour when no friend or family can come along.
verses.sanskrit_display: जहाँ हित स्वामि, न संग सखा, बनिता, सुत, बंधु, न बापु, न मैया। काय-गिरा-मनके जनके अपराध सबै छलु छाडि छमैया॥ तुलसी! तेहि काल कृपाल बिना दूजो कौन है दारुन दुःख दमैया॥ जहाँ सब संकट, दुर्घट सोचु, तहाँ मेरो साहेबु राखे रमैया॥
verses.translation: Where there is no kind master, no friend beside you, no wife, son, brother, father or mother, there is one who forgives every fault of body, word and mind, without holding back.
