Ram steps in with soft words, takes the blame on himself, and calmly points out that an old bow broke at a touch; the sage's anger finally turns to recognition.
prasangs.lesson: Clever replies feed anger; calm, humble words put it out.
prasangs.story_hook: The bow was already broken, and the man who had come to avenge it was carrying an axe.

prasangs.title_en: Janaka says goodbye to his daughter
prasangs.summary: After the wedding the time comes for Sita to leave Mithila. The palace, even the pet parrots, are in tears. Janaka, known everywhere for his detachment, holds his daughter and loses all composure; his ministers have to remind him it is time.
prasangs.lesson: Even the wisest parent breaks a little when a child leaves home; that is love.
prasangs.story_hook: He was the most detached king in the world, and his daughter was leaving.

prasangs.title_en: Ram's unease on the eve of his crowning
prasangs.summary: Dasharath, noticing grey hairs, decides to crown Ram heir, and the whole city celebrates. When Vasishtha brings Ram the news, Ram's first thought is not joy but unease: the brothers were born, raised and married together, so why should only the eldest be crowned?
prasangs.lesson: Real affection for siblings feels uneasy when one is favoured over the rest.
prasangs.story_hook: The whole city was celebrating his coronation, and Ram was thinking about his brothers.

prasangs.title_en: Manthara poisons Kaikeyi's mind
prasangs.summary: Kaikeyi is first delighted that Ram will be crowned; she loves him like her own son. Her maid Manthara works on her slowly, with sighs, hints and sweet-sounding fears about her future, until Kaikeyi believes her enemy is her only friend and goes to the sulking chamber to demand her two boons.
prasangs.lesson: Advice that flatters your fears can turn a good heart; check who benefits from it.
prasangs.story_hook: Kaikeyi was happy for Ram until her maid started to cry.

prasangs.title_en: Dasharath's two promises
prasangs.summary: Dasharath finds Kaikeyi in the sulking chamber and, eager to please her, swears by Ram to grant anything. She asks for Bharat's coronation and fourteen years of exile for Ram. Bound by his word and his love, the king spends the night begging, raging and grieving, and by morning cannot speak.
prasangs.lesson: Promise only what you have thought through; a rash vow can cost what you love most.
prasangs.story_hook: He swore by the person he loved most before he knew what she would ask.

prasangs.title_en: Ram hears he is to be exiled
prasangs.summary: Ram is called to his father's room and finds him collapsed. Kaikeyi tells him the terms. Ram smiles: his brother gets the throne, he gets to meet sages in the forest, and he can keep his father's word. Kaikeyi reads his plain words as cunning, and Ram walks out feeling, the poet says, like an elephant freed from its post.
prasangs.lesson: A lost role can be met with grace; sometimes it even feels like freedom.
prasangs.story_hook: Ram walked in expecting a crown and walked out with a forest.

prasangs.title_en: Kausalya lets her son go
prasangs.summary: Ram comes to his mother as she is preparing for his coronation. Torn between duty and love, she decides not to hold him back with 'false affection', blesses him and asks only that he not forget her. As he leaves she wonders aloud whether she will live to see his face again.
prasangs.lesson: Letting a child go with your blessing is love at its hardest.
prasangs.story_hook: She had the sweets ready for his coronation when he came to say goodbye.

prasangs.title_en: Sumitra sends Lakshman with Ram
prasangs.summary: Ram asks Lakshman to stay and care for their old father and grieving mothers; Lakshman cannot imagine life apart from him. He goes to his mother Sumitra, afraid she will stop him. Instead she tells him that home is wherever Ram is, as day is wherever the sun shines, and gives him one piece of advice for the road.
prasangs.lesson: Home is where your people are; a good send-off gives values, not just tears.
prasangs.story_hook: Lakshman went to his mother expecting to be told to stay.

prasangs.title_en: Lakshman and Guha by the sleeping Ram
prasangs.summary: On the first night of exile, Guha the boatmen's chief sees Ram and Sita sleeping on grass and weeps with anger at Kaikeyi. Lakshman, keeping watch, tells him no one gives us joy or sorrow; we live out our own actions, so don't blame anyone needlessly.
prasangs.lesson: Before blaming someone for your pain, look at the whole chain of causes, including yourself.

prasangs.title_en: Kevat washes Ram's feet
prasangs.summary: At the Ganga, a boatman refuses to take Ram across until he can wash his feet, joking that if the dust of those feet turned a stone into a woman, it might turn his boat, his family's livelihood, into one too. Ram laughs and agrees. On the far bank Sita offers her ring as fare, and Kevat refuses: after a lifetime of wages, today he has been paid in full.
prasangs.lesson: Some exchanges can't be priced; gratitude can be payment enough.
prasangs.story_hook: The boatman would not let the prince into his boat until he had washed his feet.

prasangs.title_en: Bharat comes home to grief
prasangs.summary: Bharat returns from his uncle's home to a silent city. His mother tells him proudly what she arranged; he learns his father is dead and his brother exiled because of him. Overwhelmed with shame he goes to Kausalya, expecting blame, and she embraces him as if Ram had come back, telling him not to carry the loss as his shame.
prasangs.lesson: When someone is drowning in guilt for what others did, an embrace helps more than blame.
prasangs.story_hook: Bharat came home and no one in the city would look him in the eye.

prasangs.title_en: Bharat refuses the throne
prasangs.summary: After the funeral, Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya all urge Bharat to rule, as his father wished. Bharat says the advice is right and his heart still isn't at peace; the crown means nothing without Ram. He decides to go to the forest, admit his fault, and trust his brother to forgive.
prasangs.lesson: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.
prasangs.story_hook: Everyone agreed the throne was his, and Bharat could not bring himself to sit on it.

prasangs.title_en: Guha nearly fights Bharat
prasangs.summary: Seeing Bharat's army approach the Ganga, Guha assumes he is coming to kill Ram and prepares his men to die fighting. An old man reads the omens and says Bharat comes to bring Ram back. Guha agrees that fools act in haste and repent, goes to meet Bharat with gifts, and the two embrace.
prasangs.lesson: Find out someone's intent before you prepare for war with them.
prasangs.story_hook: Guha saw an army on the riverbank and sank his boats.

prasangs.title_en: Bharadwaj lifts Bharat's shame
prasangs.summary: At Prayag Bharat meets the sage Bharadwaj, too ashamed to speak. The sage tells him not to eat himself up over his mother's deed and that what Bharat sees as a stain is a lesson for everyone. Bharat answers that he fears neither the world's talk nor the afterlife; only the thought that Ram suffers because of him keeps him awake.
prasangs.lesson: You are not your family's mistakes; carry only what is yours.
prasangs.story_hook: Bharat sat before the sage like a man hiding in his own house.

prasangs.title_en: Brihaspati checks Indra's envy
prasangs.summary: Indra, king of the gods, fears that Bharat's devotion will bring Ram back and spoil the gods' plans, and wants to trick him. His teacher Brihaspati tells him that the world runs on action, that harming a good person backfires, and that his anxiety comes from his own self-interest, not from Bharat.
prasangs.lesson: Your fear of someone else's goodness usually says more about your interests than theirs.

prasangs.title_en: Lakshman assumes the worst about Bharat
prasangs.summary: Forest dwellers report that Bharat is coming with an army. Lakshman, sure it is an attack, climbs a tree and swears to destroy him. A voice from the sky warns against acting in haste, and Ram explains that Bharat could never turn against him; power could not corrupt him.
prasangs.lesson: Think before you act on an assumption; haste turns misunderstandings into wars.
prasangs.story_hook: Lakshman saw the dust of an army and was certain he knew why it had come.

prasangs.title_en: The brothers meet at Chitrakoot
prasangs.summary: Bharat walks barefoot to Chitrakoot and falls at Ram's feet; Ram lifts him into his arms. Ram learns his father has died and grieves. When the queens arrive, Ram goes first to Kaikeyi, who caused it all, falls at her feet and comforts her, blaming no one.
prasangs.lesson: Forgiveness can mean going first to the person who hurt you and putting them at ease.
prasangs.story_hook: The first mother Ram went to was the one who had sent him away.

prasangs.title_en: The family council at Chitrakoot
prasangs.summary: Vasishtha asks how Ram can be brought home, noting that grieving people cannot judge well. Bharat recalls a brother who never broke his heart and let him win at games, and blames himself. Ram tells him his shame is needless, that love and hostility cannot be hidden, and asks him to say freely what he wants.
prasangs.lesson: In family conflict, let each speak; name love plainly; lift needless shame.

prasangs.title_en: Janaka's family joins the council
prasangs.summary: Sita's parents arrive and the two families grieve together. Kausalya tells Sunayana that people, like gold, are proved by time. Janaka asks Bharat to decide, and Bharat declines: duty and self-interest pull apart, hatred is blind and love cannot reason, so he will follow Ram's wish. His few words leave the whole court in awe.
prasangs.lesson: When you are too close to a decision, say so, and speak briefly and honestly.
prasangs.story_hook: Sita's parents walked into the forest camp, and two grieving families sat down together.

prasangs.title_en: Ram and Bharat settle it
prasangs.summary: Ram tells Bharat that keeping their father's word is the duty of both brothers, and that the leader must be like the mouth, taking in only to nourish the whole body. He asks him to rule in his place, knowing it is the harder task. Bharat accepts, asking only for Ram's sandals to keep him going.
prasangs.lesson: A good resolution gives each person a role and something to hold on to.
prasangs.story_hook: Both brothers wanted the other to be king.

prasangs.title_en: Bharat rules from a hut for fourteen years
prasangs.summary: Bharat places Ram's sandals on the throne and lives outside the city in a hut, sleeping on grass, fasting, governing only as a caretaker. The palace's riches are all around him and do not touch him, like a bee in a champak garden.
prasangs.lesson: You can live amid plenty without being owned by it.
prasangs.story_hook: For fourteen years the king of Ayodhya slept on grass outside its walls.

prasangs.title_en: Maricha caught between two deaths
prasangs.summary: Ravana orders his uncle Maricha to become a golden deer to lure Ram away. Maricha warns him that Ram cannot be defeated, but Ravana threatens him. Seeing death either way, Maricha reasons that it never pays to cross a powerful master, and chooses death at Ram's hands over death at Ravana's.
prasangs.lesson: A boss who threatens you into wrongdoing leaves no good option; see it early.
prasangs.story_hook: Whichever way he chose, Maricha knew he would not come back.

prasangs.title_en: Jatayu's last fight and Ram's grief
prasangs.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut and searches the forest, asking birds and trees if they have seen Sita. He finds the old vulture Jatayu dying; he had fought Ravana alone to stop the abduction. Ram tells him that for one whose heart is set on others' good, nothing is out of reach, and performs his funeral rites himself, as a son would.
prasangs.lesson: Standing up for someone matters, even when you cannot win.
prasangs.story_hook: He was old and half-blind, and he flew at Ravana's chariot anyway.

prasangs.title_en: Ram visits Shabari
prasangs.summary: An old forest woman, Shabari, has waited years for Ram. When he comes she washes his feet and feeds him roots and fruit, and he praises every bite. He tells her he recognises only the bond of devotion and describes nine forms of it, ending with contentment, not hunting faults, and being simple and without guile.
prasangs.lesson: What counts is the heart you bring, not who you are on paper.
prasangs.story_hook: She had swept the path every morning for years for a guest who might never come.

prasangs.title_en: Ram at Pampa on desire, anger and greed
prasangs.summary: Grieving, Ram walks with Lakshman through spring forests by Lake Pampa and describes the season as an army of desire. He names desire, anger and greed as three forces that can unsettle even the wisest mind in a moment, and notes that fruit-laden trees bow, as generous people do when they prosper.
prasangs.lesson: Desire, anger and greed can unsettle anyone; knowing that is half the defence.

prasangs.title_en: Ram tells Narada the marks of a good person
prasangs.summary: Narada asks Ram what marks a truly good person. Ram lists them: free of the six inner enemies, content, steady, generous with respect and seeking none, squirming at their own praise and glad at others', even-tempered and simple with everyone.
prasangs.lesson: Good people are uncomfortable with their own praise and glad at others'.

prasangs.title_en: Ram and Sugriva become friends
prasangs.summary: Hanuman, sent to check whether the two strangers are Bali's spies, recognises Ram and brings him to Sugriva, who has been driven out by his brother. Before a fire as witness they become friends, and Ram describes what friendship asks: your friend's small trouble is a mountain, your own is dust; steer him right, hide his faults, love him more in hard times.
prasangs.lesson: A friend treats your trouble as bigger than their own.

prasangs.title_en: Sugriva and Bali: brothers split by a misunderstanding
prasangs.summary: Bali chased a demon into a cave and told Sugriva to wait a fortnight. Sugriva waited a month; blood flowed out, he assumed Bali dead, sealed the cave and was made king. Bali fought his way out, decided his brother had betrayed him, and drove him out. Later, safe with Ram, Sugriva says that if he fought his brother even in a dream he'd be ashamed on waking.
prasangs.lesson: Brothers can become enemies over one misread moment; ask before you assume betrayal.
prasangs.story_hook: Sugriva waited outside the cave for a month, and then the blood came.

prasangs.title_en: Ram consoles Tara
prasangs.summary: After Bali's death his wife Tara weeps over his body. Ram speaks to her gently: the body is made of five elements and lies here before her, but the self is not only this body; for whom is she weeping? Comforted, she asks for devotion, and Bali's son Angad is made heir.
prasangs.lesson: Grief needs time; later, perspective on what is lost and what endures can comfort.
prasangs.story_hook: Tara knelt by her husband's body, and the man who had shot him came to sit beside her.

prasangs.title_en: Ram's monsoon and autumn lessons
prasangs.summary: Waiting out the rains on a mountain, Ram points out lessons to Lakshman in each sight: clouds bow low when full, mountains take the rain as the steady take harsh words, small streams swagger, ponds fill drop by drop, autumn sun dries the puddles as contentment dries greed, and fish panic as the water shrinks.
prasangs.lesson: Nature keeps teaching: steadiness, humility, patience, and saving for the dry season.

prasangs.title_en: Sugriva forgets his promise
prasangs.summary: The rains end and Sugriva, now king, has forgotten his promise to search for Sita. Ram is hurt; Lakshman storms into the city in anger. Hanuman had already nudged Sugriva, who comes out, admits that comfort intoxicated him, and sends search parties in every direction.
prasangs.lesson: Success and comfort make us forget who helped us; admit it quickly and make it right.
prasangs.story_hook: Sugriva had his kingdom back, and somewhere in the celebrations he forgot why.

prasangs.title_en: Sampati's burned wings
prasangs.summary: The search party, past its deadline with no news, sits down by the sea to die. A huge old vulture, Sampati, overhears them talking of his brother Jatayu. He tells them how pride once made him fly too close to the sun and burn his wings; a sage told him they would grow back when he helped Ram's messengers. He tells them where Sita is, and his wings grow back as he speaks.
prasangs.lesson: Even after the fall your pride caused, you can still be useful, and hope can return.
prasangs.story_hook: The monkeys had given up and were waiting to die when a vulture with no wings spoke to them.

prasangs.title_en: Jambavant reminds Hanuman of his strength
prasangs.summary: Nobody can leap the ocean. Old Jambavant admits honestly that he is no longer young. Then he turns to the silent Hanuman and asks why he sits quiet: what task in the world is too hard for him? Hanuman grows to the size of a mountain.
prasangs.lesson: Sometimes we need someone else to remind us what we can do; and the old can be that someone.
prasangs.story_hook: Everyone said how far they could jump, and Hanuman said nothing at all.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman meets Surasa on the way
prasangs.summary: Leaping the ocean, Hanuman refuses to rest on a friendly mountain until the work is done. Surasa blocks him and opens her jaws; he doubles his size each time she widens them, then shrinks tiny and slips in and out. A demon that catches flyers by grabbing their shadows tries the same trick, and he sees through it at once.
prasangs.lesson: Meet obstacles with flexibility: sometimes bigger, sometimes smaller, never stuck.
prasangs.story_hook: Halfway across the ocean, something opened its mouth in front of him.

prasangs.title_en: Lankini at the gate of Lanka
prasangs.summary: Entering Lanka at night as small as a mosquito, Hanuman is caught by Lankini, the city's guardian. One blow of his fist floors her; she remembers a prophecy that this means the city's end, and blesses him: a moment of good company outweighs heaven, and if he carries Ram in his heart, poison will turn to nectar.
prasangs.lesson: Carry what you love into the hard place, and the hard place changes.
prasangs.story_hook: The guard at the gate of Lanka caught a mosquito.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
prasangs.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
prasangs.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.
prasangs.story_hook: In a city of demons, Hanuman heard someone wake up and say Ram's name.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman reaches Sita
prasangs.summary: Sita, captive and threatened by Ravana, has nearly lost hope; only the guard Trijata has been kind. Hanuman drops Ram's ring from a tree, then tells her Ram's whole story. Sita says he has been her ship in a sea of separation; he gives her Ram's message that speaking of pain helps, but there is no one to tell, and asks her to wait a few days more.
prasangs.lesson: When someone is near despair, a message that they are remembered can carry them.
prasangs.story_hook: A ring fell out of the tree onto Sita's lap, and it had Ram's name on it.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman speaks plainly to Ravana
prasangs.summary: Bound and dragged before Ravana, Hanuman feels no shame and tells the most powerful man in the world, calmly, to return Sita: wealth with no deep source dries up like a rain-fed river. Ravana orders his tail set on fire; Hanuman burns Lanka and returns. Back before Ram, he insists none of it was his own greatness.
prasangs.lesson: Speak truth to power calmly, and afterwards don't take the credit.
prasangs.story_hook: They tied him up and brought him to the king, which was exactly where he wanted to be.

prasangs.title_en: Mandodari pleads, the ministers flatter
prasangs.summary: Mandodari takes Ravana aside and begs him to return Sita before it is too late. He laughs at her fear and goes to court, where his ministers tell him only what pleases him. Tulsidas notes that when advisers, doctors and teachers speak only to please, ruin comes quickly.
prasangs.lesson: Beware a circle that only tells you what you want to hear.
prasangs.story_hook: Mandodari took her husband's hand and led him somewhere the ministers couldn't hear.

prasangs.title_en: Vibhishan speaks up and is kicked
prasangs.summary: Vibhishan, bowing to his brother, advises him to return Sita: good sense and bad sense live in every heart, and Ravana is feeding the wrong one. Ravana kicks him. Vibhishan still says Ravana is like a father to him, and then he leaves, telling him not to blame him.
prasangs.lesson: Say the hard thing with respect; if you are struck for it, you may go.
prasangs.story_hook: He told his brother the truth in front of the whole court, and his brother kicked him.

prasangs.title_en: Vibhishan crosses over
prasangs.summary: Vibhishan crosses the sea to Ram. Sugriva suspects a spy; Ram says he never turns away anyone who comes for refuge, and that only a clean heart, without deceit, reaches him. He embraces Vibhishan, asks how he kept his goodness among the wicked, and crowns him king of Lanka before the war has even begun.
prasangs.lesson: Leaving a bad place takes courage; a good leader receives people without suspicion first.
prasangs.story_hook: Vibhishan arrived at the enemy camp with nothing but his name.

prasangs.title_en: Three days at the ocean: humble first, firm after
prasangs.summary: On Vibhishan's advice, Ram first asks the ocean politely to let his army cross, and waits three days. When nothing changes, he takes up his bow, observing that counsel to the unwilling is like seed on barren soil. The ocean appears, apologises, and shows him how to build a bridge.
prasangs.lesson: Always ask humbly first. But don't let humility be taken for weakness.
prasangs.story_hook: Ram sat on the shore and asked the ocean, politely, to move.

prasangs.title_en: Mandodari and Prahasta warn Ravana again
prasangs.summary: Mandodari, hearing the bridge is built, again begs Ravana to pick fights only where he can win, and to step back. Ravana boasts. His son Prahasta tells the court that flatterers are many and honest advisers few, and suggests first sending an envoy. Ravana insults him, and Prahasta leaves saying good advice cannot reach one set on ruin.
prasangs.lesson: Some people cannot hear good advice; give it, then stop beating yourself up.
prasangs.story_hook: The bridge was built, the army was across, and the king of Lanka was still laughing.

prasangs.title_en: Angad in Ravana's court
prasangs.summary: Ram sends Angad as envoy, asking him to speak so the work gets done and it does Ravana good too. In court Ravana insults Angad, his dead father and his lord. Angad bears it, remembering that a lion gains no glory by killing a jackal. At last he plants his foot and dares anyone to move it; no warrior can.
prasangs.lesson: Under insult, keep your purpose; a steady mind does not leave what is right.
prasangs.story_hook: Angad sat down in the enemy's court, and they began to insult his father.

prasangs.title_en: Lakshman falls; Hanuman brings the mountain
prasangs.summary: Lakshman is struck down by Meghnad's spear. The physician Sushena names a herb on a far mountain, and Hanuman races there, sees through a demon disguised as a sage, and, not recognising the herb, carries the whole peak. Over Ayodhya Bharat shoots him down by mistake, then revives him and helps him on. At midnight Ram holds Lakshman and grieves aloud for a brother who left everything for him; Hanuman arrives just in time.
prasangs.lesson: When someone you love is ill, urgency and hope go together.
prasangs.story_hook: It was past midnight, Lakshman was not breathing, and Hanuman had not come back.

prasangs.title_en: Kumbhakarna fights for a brother he knows is wrong
prasangs.summary: Woken to fight, Kumbhakarna tells Ravana plainly he was wrong to take Sita and should have consulted him first. Still he goes out to fight for his brother. On the field he meets Vibhishan, who chose Ram, and instead of cursing him, he blesses him as the pride of their family.
prasangs.lesson: Siblings can choose differently and still bless each other.
prasangs.story_hook: Kumbhakarna woke up, heard what his brother had done, and told him he was wrong.

prasangs.title_en: The chariot that wins
prasangs.summary: Ravana rides out in a chariot; Ram stands on foot, and Vibhishan worries. Ram describes the chariot that really wins: courage and patience as its wheels, truth and character as its flag, strength, judgement, self-control and kindness as its horses.
prasangs.lesson: Inner qualities are the real equipment for a hard fight.

prasangs.title_en: Ram hurries home
prasangs.summary: After the war, Vibhishan begs Ram to stay a while, bathe and rest in Lanka's palaces. Ram says all of it is his as much as Vibhishan's, but thinking of Bharat waiting at home, each moment feels like an age; if he is late, he may not find his brother alive.
prasangs.lesson: When someone at home is waiting, no comfort elsewhere can hold you.
prasangs.story_hook: The war was won, the palace was his, and all Ram wanted was to go home.

prasangs.title_en: The last day of waiting
prasangs.summary: One day is left of the fourteen years and there is no word. Bharat wonders whether Ram has forgotten him, and his mind starts to sink. Just then Hanuman arrives like a boat and says Ram is coming. Bharat says no gift could repay this news.
prasangs.lesson: Waiting is hardest on the last day; hope can arrive just as you go under.
prasangs.story_hook: There was one day left, and Bharat had begun to wonder whether he had been forgotten.

prasangs.title_en: Ram comes home
prasangs.summary: From the air Ram points out his birthplace, dearer to him than heaven. Bharat falls at his feet; Ram lifts him up and the mothers run to him like cows to their calves at dusk. Ram introduces his friends as those who carried him through the war, and seeing Kaikeyi ashamed, goes to her house first.
prasangs.lesson: Homecoming means gratitude to those who carried you and kindness to those ashamed to face you.
prasangs.story_hook: From the air, Ram could see the river of the town where he was born.

prasangs.title_en: Ram says goodbye to his friends
prasangs.summary: After six happy months, Ram sends his monkey and bear friends home with gifts. Angad, whose father is dead, begs to stay: Ram is his father and mother now. Ram embraces him and sends him on. To the boatman Guha he says: you are a brother to me; keep visiting.
prasangs.lesson: Friendships made in hard times deserve to be kept; say so out loud.
prasangs.story_hook: The war was over, and Angad did not want to go home.

prasangs.title_en: Ram on good people and difficult people
prasangs.summary: Bharat asks Ram to explain the difference between good and malicious people. Ram says the good are like sandalwood that perfumes the axe that cuts it; they feel others' sorrow and joy as their own and never speak harshly. The malicious burn at others' success and feast on gossip. No duty equals doing good to others.
prasangs.lesson: Do good, feel others' joy as your own, and refuse the pleasure of gossip.

prasangs.title_en: Ram's address to the citizens
prasangs.summary: Ram calls his people together and says he speaks without pride of rank: if he says anything wrong, stop him without fear. The way he recommends needs no grand effort, only a simple nature, an honest mind, contentment, and no grudges, no quarrels, no craving and no fear.
prasangs.lesson: A good leader invites correction; a good life is simple, honest and free of grudges.

prasangs.title_en: Garuda's doubt
prasangs.summary: Garuda, Vishnu's own mount, frees Ram from a serpent-noose in battle and starts to doubt: how can God be bound? He goes to Narada, Brahma and Shiva, who sends him to an old crow, Kakbhushundi, saying doubts clear only with long time in good company. Kakbhushundi tells him no one has escaped delusion, desire, craving or anger; Garuda ends up grateful for the doubt that led him there.
prasangs.lesson: Doubt is human; stay long enough in good company and it can lead somewhere better.
prasangs.story_hook: The great eagle Garuda flew to a crow to ask a question.

prasangs.title_en: Kakbhushundi and the child Ram
prasangs.summary: Kakbhushundi used to visit Ayodhya to watch Ram as a child. Once he doubted that a toddler chasing a crow could be God; Ram reached for him across every world, and he saw universes inside the child's mouth. Humbled, he was offered every power and chose devotion, since comforts without it are a feast without salt. Ram explains that pride is lanced from those he loves, as a mother lances a child's boil.
prasangs.lesson: Pride is taken from us painfully, for our good; what remains is what matters.
prasangs.story_hook: The crow kept stealing scraps from a toddler in a palace courtyard, until the toddler reached for him.

prasangs.title_en: The student who would not stand for his teacher
prasangs.summary: In an earlier life Kakbhushundi was a proud, wealthy, sharp-tongued young man whose gentle teacher kept trying to guide him. One day in the temple he refused even to rise when the teacher entered. The teacher said nothing, but a curse fell on the student; the teacher at once prayed for him, asking that he not be punished in anger. Lives later, the one thorn Kakbhushundi still carries is the memory of that teacher's gentleness.
prasangs.lesson: Respect those who teach you; and forgive like the teacher who prayed for his rude student.
prasangs.story_hook: The teacher walked into the temple, and his student did not get up.

prasangs.title_en: Arguing with Lomash
prasangs.summary: As a young seeker Kakbhushundi went to the sage Lomash, who taught the formless God; Kakbhushundi kept arguing for his own view until the sage, provoked again and again, lost his temper and cursed him to become a crow. Kakbhushundi took it without fear or self-pity, and the sage, regretting his anger, called him back and taught him the Ramcharitmanas.
prasangs.lesson: Even calm people burn when pushed too far; take correction without bitterness.
prasangs.story_hook: He kept arguing with the old sage, long after he should have stopped.

prasangs.title_en: Garuda's seven questions
prasangs.summary: Garuda asks seven questions: the rarest body, the greatest sorrow and joy, the nature of good and wicked people, the highest virtue and the worst wrong, and the diseases of the mind. Kakbhushundi answers: no sorrow like want, no joy like meeting good people; non-harm is highest and slander worst; delusion is the root disease, with lust, greed, anger, envy and ego as its symptoms.
prasangs.lesson: Know your mind's diseases by name: confusion, anger, greed, envy, ego.

prasangs.title_en: Ram at the ocean: humble first, firm after
prasangs.summary: Ram lies on kusha grass by the shore for three days, asking the ocean for a way. Ignored, he tells Lakshman that patience is being taken for weakness and takes up his bow. The ocean rises, offers a way (Nala's bridge), and Ram releases the arrow elsewhere at its request.
prasangs.lesson: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.
prasangs.story_hook: For three days the prince lay on a bed of grass at the edge of the sea, asking politely.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: On fools and the half-learned
prasangs.summary: Twelve verses on the futility of arguing with the closed or half-educated mind, framed as satire. The poet admits his own early arrogance (Niti 8) and ends by preferring wild mountains to the company of fools.
prasangs.lesson: Spend your effort where it can land; some minds will not move, and the first one to check is yours.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: In praise of learning and the learned
prasangs.summary: Bhartrihari praises learning as wealth no thief can take and speech as the one lasting ornament, then turns to good company and the three kinds of people who face obstacles. It ends with the 'sword's-edge vow' of the good.
prasangs.lesson: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: Honour and spirit
prasangs.summary: Images of the lion and the elephant celebrate self-respect and inborn spirit. Some verses lean toward intolerance of insult, a warrior-king ideal.
prasangs.lesson: Keep your dignity without needing to win every fight.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasangs.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasangs.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the wicked
prasangs.summary: A field guide to toxic people: the brilliant but cruel, the spiteful critic who turns every virtue into a fault, the boss nobody can please, and friendships that shrink like morning shade.
prasangs.lesson: Recognise spite for what it is, keep your distance, and stop taking it personally.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the good
prasangs.summary: Portraits of good people: steady in trouble, humble in success, giving in secret and speaking of others' kindness aloud. Company, the verses say, makes us what we are.
prasangs.lesson: Be soft in good times and firm in bad ones, and let your good deeds stay quiet.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: On helping others
prasangs.summary: Verses on generosity and friendship: trees bow with fruit, the hand shines by giving, a true friend keeps you from wrong and stays in trouble. Four kinds of people, from the selfless to those who harm for nothing.
prasangs.lesson: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasangs.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasangs.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: On fate
prasangs.summary: Bhartrihari voices the case for fate with fables (Indra defeated, the rat that fed a starving snake, the bald man under the palm). Even here he insists one should still act after careful thought.
prasangs.lesson: Not everything is in your hands; that is a reason to act wisely, not to stop acting.

prasangs.title_en: Nitishatakam: On action
prasangs.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasangs.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasangs.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasangs.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: The mockery of giving up pleasures
prasangs.summary: Pleasures will leave us anyway; letting them go freely brings peace, being dragged from them brings torment. We are worse than the moth, because we know the flame burns.
prasangs.lesson: Let go before you are forced to, and stop calling relief happiness.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of begging and servility
prasangs.summary: On the humiliation of begging favours from the rich: only hungry children could make a proud man ask. Contentment, not wealth, is real joy.
prasangs.lesson: Keep your dignity; ask for help for others before you ever grovel for yourself.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the instability of pleasures
prasangs.summary: Everything carries its own fear, health is uprooted, life leaks like water from a cracked pot. Only dispassion is fearless.
prasangs.lesson: Everything you hold carries fear; hold it more lightly.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
prasangs.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
prasangs.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Dialogue between the ascetic and the king
prasangs.summary: An ascetic tells a king who ignores him that learning equals wealth, that contentment in bark equals contentment in silk, and that pride over a few towns is a fever.
prasangs.lesson: When the mind is content, nobody is richer than you.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Advice to the mind
prasangs.summary: The poet talks to his own mind: why exhaust yourself pleasing others, why replay the past and script the future, why roam everywhere but within. 'So what?' asks what all our gains amount to.
prasangs.lesson: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Weighing the lasting and the passing
prasangs.summary: Weighing what lasts: religion without inner peace is trading; old age can bring neglect; act while healthy, not when the house is on fire. The poet admits not knowing how to spend a short life.
prasangs.lesson: Do what matters most while you still can.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Worship of Shiva
prasangs.summary: Devotional verses longing for a quiet life by the Ganga in Shiva's presence, including a famous non-sectarian line that Shiva and Vishnu are one in essence.
prasangs.lesson: Gratitude for a simple life, and devotion without rivalry between forms of God.

prasangs.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: The way of the free ascetic
prasangs.summary: Portraits of the wandering sage: unbothered when people argue over his caste, sleeping under the sky like a king, and finally bidding farewell to the five elements.
prasangs.lesson: Let others' labels and small things pass; contentment makes you rich.

prasangs.title_en: The fruit of immortality (legend of Bhartrihari's renunciation)
prasangs.summary: A legend, not history. A poor brahmin is given a fruit of immortality and, thinking a long life of poverty useless, gives it to King Bhartrihari of Ujjain. The king gives it to his beloved queen; it passes from lover to lover and returns to his hands. Heartbroken, he speaks 'yam cintayami' (Niti 2), hands the throne to his brother Vikrama and becomes a renunciant.
prasangs.lesson: Betrayal can break you, or it can wake you up to what lasts.
prasangs.story_hook: A poor brahmin in Ujjain held a fruit that could make him immortal, and wondered what a long life of begging was worth.

prasangs.title_en: Karunya stops acting: knowledge and action as two wings
prasangs.summary: A student asks the sage Agastya whether freedom comes from action or from knowledge. Agastya answers with a story: young Karunya, confused by two scriptures, simply stopped doing anything, and his father had to show him that understanding and action work together.
prasangs.lesson: Don't freeze while you wait to be sure. Understanding and action have to fly together.
prasangs.story_hook: Karunya came home from his studies so full of questions that he stopped doing anything at all.

prasangs.title_en: Rama comes home from his pilgrimage and loses interest in everything
prasangs.summary: Sixteen-year-old Rama returns from a long pilgrimage and quietly withdraws: he stops eating properly, stops laughing, ignores his duties and sits alone. His attendants tell the worried king. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha say this is not illness or weakness but the first stirring of real questions, and ask that Rama be brought to them.
prasangs.lesson: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.
prasangs.story_hook: The prince who had everything came back from his travels and stopped laughing.

prasangs.title_en: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasangs.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasangs.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.
prasangs.story_hook: In front of the whole court, the young prince stood up and said what everyone feels and nobody says.

prasangs.title_en: Rama asks how to live in the world without being crushed by it
prasangs.summary: After his lament Rama turns to questions. How did King Janaka and others stay free while running kingdoms? How can a person work in the world untouched, like water on a lotus leaf? He asks for one practical skill that lets him work without sorrow.
prasangs.lesson: The real question isn't whether to quit life, but how to live it without being swallowed.
prasangs.story_hook: Having said what was wrong, Rama finally asked the question that matters: how do the wise do it?

prasangs.title_en: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasangs.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasangs.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

prasangs.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasangs.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasangs.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

prasangs.title_en: Queen Lila fears losing her husband
prasangs.summary: Queen Lila loves her husband so much that she cannot bear the thought of his death. The wise tell her that nothing wins immortality, so she prays to the goddess Sarasvati instead. When the king dies, Sarasvati begins to show her that life and death are not what they seem.
prasangs.lesson: Love brings the fear of loss; trying to control death only deepens the fear.
prasangs.story_hook: Queen Lila was so happy with her husband that one night she was seized by the thought of losing him.

prasangs.title_en: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasangs.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasangs.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
prasangs.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.

prasangs.title_en: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
prasangs.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.
prasangs.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.
prasangs.story_hook: When their parents died, one brother quietly lit the funeral fires and the other ran weeping into the forest.

prasangs.title_en: Bali tires of endless days and asks his father's riddle
prasangs.summary: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day at his window he realises he is doing the same things day after day, night after night, and asks what any of it adds up to. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him: a vast realm ruled by a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind; win it over, by practice, and everything is won.
prasangs.lesson: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.
prasangs.story_hook: Bali had conquered everything there was to conquer, and one evening he realised he was bored.

prasangs.title_en: Prahlada: effort and grace are not rivals
prasangs.summary: After telling how Prahlada awakened, Vasishtha faces Rama's challenge: if everything comes by effort, wasn't Prahlada saved by Vishnu's grace? Vasishtha answers that Prahlada earned it himself, that the Self and Vishnu are not two, and that sometimes we wake by our own effort and sometimes by grace reached through devotion. Steady daily practice ripens the mind like a mango.
prasangs.lesson: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.

prasangs.title_en: Two old friends meet again and admit they never found peace
prasangs.summary: Bhasa and Vilasa grow up inseparable in a forest hermitage. After their fathers die they drift apart and spend long lonely years in hard austerities. When they meet again as old men, one asks if the other is well; he answers honestly that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries.
prasangs.lesson: Years of hard effort without inner understanding can leave you exactly where you started.
prasangs.story_hook: They had been inseparable as boys, and when they met again they were old men with nothing to show.

prasangs.title_en: Bhushunda, the crow who outlived the ages
prasangs.summary: Vasishtha travels to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has watched world-ages come and go. Asked how he has lived so long, untroubled, Bhushunda lists his habits: he doesn't brood on the past or future, doesn't fret about what he'll get next, doesn't grow arrogant from knowing, and shares in others' joys and sorrows.
prasangs.lesson: A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind.
prasangs.story_hook: High on a mountain lived a crow who had watched whole ages of the world rise and fall.

prasangs.title_en: Queen Chudala teaches her husband what renunciation really is
prasangs.summary: Queen Chudala finds inner peace, but her husband, King Shikhidhvaja, doesn't believe her. Restless, he leaves his kingdom for the forest. Chudala rules wisely in his absence and visits him disguised as a young sage, Kumbha, who shows him that giving up kingdom, home and body is not renunciation; letting go of the clinging mind is. Freed, he returns home and rules beside her.
prasangs.lesson: Running away doesn't free you; letting go inside does. Sometimes the teacher is the person beside you.
prasangs.story_hook: The queen had found peace, and the king, who loved her, could not believe it.

prasangs.title_en: Shiva's three vows: be a great doer, enjoyer and letter-go
prasangs.summary: Vasishtha gives Rama three vows that Shiva once gave his devotee Bhringi: be a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer. A great doer acts fully and on time without clinging; a great enjoyer takes in joys and sorrows evenly, like the ocean takes in rivers; a great renouncer lets go inside. Live this way and work won't wear you out.
prasangs.lesson: Work fully, enjoy fully, let go fully; anchored inside, you can do it all without burning out.

prasangs.title_en: 'Sisters and Brothers of America': Chicago, 11 September 1893
prasangs.summary: An unknown 30-year-old monk from India, with no invitation and little money, rises on the Parliament's opening day and greets the hall as 'Sisters and Brothers of America'. The audience stands and applauds for minutes. In a five-minute address he says India's faith accepts all religions as true and hopes the day marks the death-knell of fanaticism.
prasangs.lesson: You can belong fully to your own tradition and still honour every other path.
prasangs.story_hook: On 11 September 1893, a young Indian monk with no formal invitation stood up in Chicago and said five words that brought the hall to its feet.
characters: Delegates and audience of the World's Parliament of Religions

prasangs.title_en: The frog in the well (Chicago, 15 September 1893)
prasangs.summary: Asked why religions quarrel, he tells of a frog who has lived all its life in a well. When a frog from the sea arrives and describes the ocean, the well-frog refuses to believe anything can be bigger than his well and drives the visitor out. Each of us, he says, sits in a little well and calls it the world.
prasangs.lesson: Before you judge another faith or culture, check the size of your own well.
prasangs.story_hook: A frog lived in a well so long that he was sure the well was the whole world, until one day a frog from the sea fell in.
characters: A frog born in a well

prasangs.title_en: 'Children of immortal bliss': the Paper on Hinduism (Chicago, 19 September 1893)
prasangs.summary: In his main paper he explains Hindu ideas to an American audience that had heard them mostly from critics. He refuses to call anyone a sinner, quoting the Upanishad's 'children of immortal bliss', and describes religions as stages of one search, travelling 'from truth to truth'.
prasangs.lesson: You are not a sinner to be fixed; you are a soul to be uncovered.
prasangs.story_hook: When Vivekananda read his paper in Chicago, many listeners had only heard of Hinduism from missionaries, and he began by refusing to call any of them sinners.

prasangs.title_en: 'Help and not fight': the closing address (Chicago, 27 September 1893)
prasangs.summary: On the last day he says no one should hope for unity through one religion's triumph. A seed takes in earth, air and water but grows into its own plant; so each faith should take in the others' spirit and grow by its own law.
prasangs.lesson: Take in what is good from others, and keep growing as yourself.
prasangs.story_hook: On the Parliament's final evening, Vivekananda held up a seed to explain how a person can absorb a new world without losing himself.

prasangs.title_en: Karma-Yoga 1: how work makes character
prasangs.summary: He defines karma as work and says character is the sum of the impressions our actions leave. Misery teaches as much as joy, and character shows in small daily actions, not big moments. The ideal worker finds calm in the middle of intense activity.
prasangs.lesson: Character is built in ordinary actions, and you are building it right now.

prasangs.title_en: Karma-Yoga 2: each is great in his own place
prasangs.summary: Duty differs from person to person, so no one should be judged by another's standard. Hating yourself for not meeting someone else's ideal only weakens you. He ends with the story of a king who learns that the householder and the monk are each great in their own place.
prasangs.lesson: Measure yourself by your own ideal, not by someone else's.
prasangs.story_hook: A king kept asking who was greater, the monk or the householder, until a young sannyasin offered to show him.

prasangs.title_en: Karma-Yoga 3: the secret of work
prasangs.summary: The Gita's central idea is to work hard without being attached. Selfish work is slave's work; real love brings no pain; giving without expecting a return frees us. He closes with the Mahabharata story of the mongoose and the poor family's gift.
prasangs.lesson: Work like a master, not a slave; give without keeping accounts.

prasangs.title_en: Karma-Yoga 4: what is duty?
prasangs.summary: Duty cannot be defined from outside, since customs differ, so we should see others' duties through their eyes. Duty becomes sweet only through love, and small irritations are best met by forbearance. He passes on Pavhari Baba's secret: join the end and the means into one.
prasangs.lesson: See others through their own eyes, and let love turn duty into something lighter.

prasangs.title_en: The proud ascetic, the housewife and the butcher
prasangs.summary: A young ascetic who can burn a bird with a glance is humbled by a housewife who knows what he did, and she sends him to a butcher in the market for teaching. The butcher, doing his trade honestly and caring for his parents, teaches him the highest truth. Doing the duty in front of you, without attachment, is itself the path.
prasangs.lesson: No honest work is beneath you; doing it well is the practice.
prasangs.story_hook: A young yogi glared at a crow and it fell dead, and for the rest of the day he was sure he had become a very great man.

prasangs.title_en: Karma-Yoga 5: we help ourselves, not the world
prasangs.summary: The world does not need our help; helping is a privilege that makes us stronger. Expecting thanks brings unhappiness, so be grateful to the one you help. The world is a moral gymnasium, and calm people do the best work.
prasangs.lesson: Helping is a privilege, not a debt someone owes you.

prasangs.title_en: Karma-Yoga 6: non-attachment
prasangs.summary: All work mixes good and evil, so the way out is not to stop working but to stop clinging. The belief that others depend on us is the root of attachment and pain. Stand as a witness and keep working.
prasangs.lesson: Care fully, but let go of the idea that everything depends on you.

prasangs.title_en: Karma-Yoga 7: freedom
prasangs.summary: Misery comes from attachment, not work. He attacks duty that has become a compulsion and asks for work done freely. The greatest people often die unknown, so seek no praise.
prasangs.lesson: Be at rest, be free, and work.

prasangs.title_en: Karma-Yoga 8: the ideal of Karma-Yoga
prasangs.summary: Every path, whether work, love, meditation or knowledge, leads to the same freedom. Do not flee the world-machine; learn the secret of work from inside it. He holds up the Buddha as the ideal worker who acted without personal motive.
prasangs.lesson: You don't have to escape your life to find peace; learn to work inside it.

prasangs.title_en: The drunken monkey: taming a restless mind
prasangs.summary: The mind is a monkey made drunk by desire, stung by jealousy and possessed by pride. The first practice is to sit and watch it without fighting; each day it grows calmer. Then take up one idea and let it fill your life.
prasangs.lesson: Watch the mind before trying to control it; calm comes with daily practice.
prasangs.story_hook: There was a monkey, restless as all monkeys are; someone gave it wine, then a scorpion stung it, and then a demon got into it.

prasangs.title_en: 'This is the whole of religion'
prasangs.summary: In one paragraph he sums up his teaching: each soul is potentially divine, and the goal is to bring that out through work, worship, mental discipline or philosophy. Doctrines, rituals, books and temples are secondary.
prasangs.lesson: Religion is growth from within; forms are helpers, not the point.

prasangs.title_en: Work and its secret (Los Angeles, 1900)
prasangs.summary: His greatest lesson, he says, was to attend to the means as much as the end. Most failures come from neglecting the means, and most sorrow from clinging to what is already failing. Weakness invites misery, yet a heart that refuses to love also loses life's joys.
prasangs.lesson: Look after the means; keep the power to let go.

prasangs.title_en: Practical Vedanta 1: faith in yourself (London, 1896)
prasangs.summary: Vedanta must work in ordinary life. Calm minds do the most work, angry ones break themselves. The new religion calls the person who does not believe in himself the atheist, and the remedy for weakness is to think of strength, not brood over weakness.
prasangs.lesson: Stop rehearsing your weakness; think of your strength and act.

prasangs.title_en: Practical Vedanta 2: the temple of the human body
prasangs.summary: Retelling Upanishadic stories such as Satyakama's, he argues that God is to be seen in every person. Real help comes from within, and we should look at others with sympathy, since they walk the road we walked.
prasangs.lesson: Treat the person in front of you as sacred.

prasangs.title_en: Practical Vedanta 4: mistakes and light
prasangs.summary: He admits he has made many mistakes and would not be who he is without them. Weeping over darkness does not remove it; striking a match does. Build character instead of brooding over past wrongs.
prasangs.lesson: Don't mourn the darkness; strike a match.

prasangs.title_en: Cups, jars and buckets: the ideal of a universal religion
prasangs.summary: Truth can be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, like water taking the shape of each vessel. His plan is 'Do not destroy': help if you can, never attack sincere convictions. No one can make another spiritual, just as no one makes a plant grow; we can only remove obstacles.
prasangs.lesson: Let each person, and each child, grow in their own shape.
prasangs.story_hook: Imagine everyone going to the same lake with a cup, a jar or a bucket, and arguing about the shape of water.

prasangs.title_en: Many photographs of one sun (Pasadena, 1900)
prasangs.summary: Speaking in a Universalist church, he welcomes sects because difference is a sign of thinking. Truth seen from different standpoints looks different, like photographs of one church from four corners. Spiritual ideas must reach each person in their own language.
prasangs.lesson: Disagreement between thinking people is natural, not a threat.

prasangs.title_en: Nachiketa and the razor's edge (London, 1896)
prasangs.summary: He reads the Katha Upanishad to a London audience: the boy Nachiketa, sent to Death, refuses every reward until he learns what lies beyond death. The path is like a razor's edge, long and hard, but he urges: struggle on, awake, arise.
prasangs.lesson: The way is long; don't despair, keep walking.

prasangs.title_en: Never mind failures (London, 1896)
prasangs.summary: Fill the mind with the highest thoughts. Failures are natural, even the beauty of life; hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, try once more.
prasangs.lesson: Failure is part of the path; try once more.

prasangs.title_en: Homecoming in Calcutta: 'Be not afraid' (1897)
prasangs.summary: Back in his home city after four years in the West, he tells the young men of Calcutta that fear is the greatest superstition and fearlessness brings heaven in a moment. He ends with the Katha Upanishad's call, arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.
prasangs.lesson: Fear is the main obstacle; act without it.

prasangs.title_en: 'Awake from this hypnotism of weakness' (Kumbakonam, 1897)
prasangs.summary: In South India on his return, he quotes Katha 1.3.14 in Sanskrit and renders it 'Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached'. He asks his listeners to wake from the hypnotism of weakness, since no one is really weak.
prasangs.lesson: Arise, awake: no one is really weak.

prasangs.title_en: Learn from all, imitate none (Lahore, 1897)
prasangs.summary: Speaking to rival reform and orthodox groups, he looks for common ground. Religion must be realised, not repeated like a parrot. Learn everything good from others, as a seed takes in earth, air and water, but grow into your own tree and do not become others.
prasangs.lesson: Absorb the best of where you live, and grow into yourself.

prasangs.title_en: 'Whatever you think, that you will be' (Jaffna, 1897)
prasangs.summary: On his first tour after the West he summarises Vedanta for the Hindus of Jaffna. Thinking yourself weak makes you weak; children should be raised strong and told of the glory of the soul. Learn to serve before you lead.
prasangs.lesson: Thoughts shape us, so teach yourself and your children strength.

prasangs.title_en: 'Reject it as poison' (Madras, 1897)
prasangs.summary: He answers critics who claimed others made his American success, noting how quickly sympathy vanishes when you dare to differ. His test of truth: whatever makes you weak in body, mind or spirit, reject as poison.
prasangs.lesson: Judge ideas, and habits, by whether they make you stronger.

prasangs.title_en: 'To my brave boys' (letter from New York, 1894)
prasangs.summary: Writing to his young supporters in Madras, he says love, sincerity and patience are all they need. Struggle was his motto in the dark and still is in the light. Be the servant while leading, never listen to gossip about a friend, and have infinite patience.
prasangs.lesson: Lead by serving, refuse gossip, and keep struggling.

prasangs.title_en: Ridicule, opposition, acceptance (letter to Khetri, 1895)
prasangs.summary: Facing opposition from some clergy in America, he writes to his friend the Maharaja that every work passes through ridicule, opposition and then acceptance. Anyone ahead of their time will be misunderstood, so he will stay steady.
prasangs.lesson: Ridicule and opposition are stages, not verdicts.

prasangs.title_en: 'Read the last lines whenever you feel worried or jealous' (1896)
prasangs.summary: The day before sailing for England, he sends a young doctor starting a magazine a few lines: go on bravely, don't expect success in a day or a year, hold to the highest, avoid jealousy. He tells him to reread them whenever worry or jealousy returns.
prasangs.lesson: Expect slow success, stay steady, and drop jealousy.

prasangs.title_en: A letter to a grieving friend (Bombay, 1893)
prasangs.summary: Just before sailing for America, he writes to a friend struck by a terrible family loss. Quoting Job, Jesus and the Gita, he says that under the waves there is a depth of calm. He also admits the heart's agony fights against resignation, and prays for strength.
prasangs.lesson: Under the storm of grief there is a deeper calm; it is all right that the heart resists.

prasangs.title_en: 'I am drifting': a letter from Alameda (1900)
prasangs.summary: Two years before his death, worn out, he writes that he has laid down the role of leader. He is glad he was born, glad he suffered, glad he made big blunders. He admits that ambition, personality, fear and love of power lay behind his work, and says they are fading as he drifts toward peace.
prasangs.lesson: Honest looking back, with gratitude for the mistakes, can bring peace.

prasangs.title_en: 'Hold on yet a while, brave heart' (poem to the Maharaja of Khetri)
prasangs.summary: A short poem of encouragement to a friend. Clouds hide the sun for a while, summer always follows winter, and no honest struggle is wasted even when hopes fail.
prasangs.lesson: No struggle is wasted; hold on a little longer.

prasangs.title_en: 'Requiescat in pace': for J. J. Goodwin (1898)
prasangs.summary: When his English stenographer and devoted friend Goodwin died young in India, he wrote this farewell. It sends the soul on with blessing and says sweet remembrance fills the place left behind.
prasangs.lesson: Love can bless the one who has gone and let memory fill the gap.

prasangs.title_en: Concentration and detachment
prasangs.summary: All success depends on concentration, but along with it we must build the power to detach, since most suffering comes from a mind stuck on something it cannot let go. If he were educated again, he would train concentration and detachment rather than collect facts.
prasangs.lesson: Train the mind to focus and to let go; both matter.

prasangs.title_en: Inspired Talks at Thousand Island Park (June 1895)
prasangs.summary: In a summer retreat on an island in the St. Lawrence River, he taught a dozen students daily; Sarah Ellen Waldo took notes. Short sayings: thoughts live and travel far, so guard them; neither seek nor avoid, take what comes.
prasangs.lesson: Guard your thoughts; take what comes without clutching.
characters: A small group of American disciples

prasangs.title_en: Vibhishan crosses over: Ram's refuge speech
prasangs.summary: Kicked out of Lanka for telling his brother the truth, Vibhishan crosses the sea to Ram, dreaming of his feet. Sugriva wants him bound as a spy; Ram says his vow is to remove the fear of anyone who comes for refuge, and if the visitor were truly wicked he would not have come at all. Ram embraces him, asks how he kept his goodness among the cruel, describes the devotee who ties every thread of love to him, and crowns him king, shyly giving what Ravana got for ten heads.
prasangs.lesson: The turning itself is enough to be taken in; your past is not the deciding question.
prasangs.story_hook: Kicked out by his own brother, a man stood on the far shore and wondered whether the enemy he was walking toward would let him in.

prasangs.title_en: Valmiki: Ram's vow of refuge and the dove
prasangs.summary: Vibhishana arrives in the sky over Ram's camp. Sugriva argues he should be killed as a spy; Hanuman and Ram disagree. Ram tells the story of a dove that sheltered the hunter who had caught its mate, cites the sage Kandu on protecting whoever asks for shelter, and makes his vow: whoever comes once and says 'I am yours' gets safety from all beings, even if it were Ravana himself.
prasangs.lesson: Refuge is a vow, not a reward for the deserving: once someone says 'I'm yours', they are safe.
prasangs.story_hook: The monkey king wanted the stranger killed; Ram answered with a story about a dove.

prasangs.title_en: Kevat washes Ram's feet
prasangs.summary: At the Ganga the boatman refuses to row Ram across unless he can first wash his feet, joking that their dust turned a stone into a woman and might turn his boat into one too. Ram, whose name carries the world across, smiles and pleads with him. Afterwards the boatman refuses Sita's ring: today, he says, he has been paid in full.
prasangs.lesson: Love can be playful and stubborn; God enjoys being loved that way.
prasangs.story_hook: The boatman folded his arms and told the prince of Ayodhya he was not getting into his boat until he let him wash his feet.

prasangs.title_en: Shabari's wait and the nine forms of devotion
prasangs.summary: An old woman of the forest has waited years for Ram on her teacher's word. When he comes she falls at his feet, washes them, and feeds him fruit he praises again and again. She says she does not know how to praise him; he answers that he recognises only the kinship of devotion, teaches her the nine forms of devotion, and tells her that whoever has even one of them is most dear to him.
prasangs.lesson: Your simple offering is enough; love, not status, is the only kinship that counts.
prasangs.story_hook: For years an old woman swept the path and gathered fruit for a guest she had been told would come.

prasangs.title_en: Jatayu dies in Ram's lap
prasangs.summary: Searching for Sita, Ram finds the old vulture who fought Ravana to save her, dying. Ram touches his head and the bird's pain leaves. Jatayu refuses Ram's offer to heal him: the one whose name people pray to say at death is in front of his eyes. He asks only for devotion, and Ram, in tears, performs his last rites with his own hands.
prasangs.lesson: Nothing you do for love is small; it is honoured like family.
prasangs.story_hook: An old bird lay broken on the forest floor, holding on to life just long enough to tell Ram what he had seen.

prasangs.title_en: Valmiki: Ram cremates Jatayu like his father
prasangs.summary: Jatayu dies telling Ram where Ravana went. Ram says this loss weighs on him more than Sita's abduction, that the bird is as worthy of honour as his father Dasharatha, builds the pyre himself and performs the rites as for his own kin.
prasangs.lesson: Grief for a loyal friend, even a bird, is real grief; honour it fully.
prasangs.story_hook: Ram had just lost his wife, and yet what broke him that afternoon was the death of an old bird.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman meets Ram
prasangs.summary: Sent by a frightened Sugriva, Hanuman goes disguised as a brahmin to question two strangers. When Ram names himself, Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet speechless, then gently complains that Ram forgot him. He says he knows no method of worship and relies on Ram as a child relies on its mother. Ram lifts him up, holds him, cools him with his own tears, and tells him he is twice as dear as Lakshman.
prasangs.lesson: You don't need the right method; being his is enough, and he weeps to have you back.
prasangs.story_hook: On a mountain path, a monkey in disguise asked two strangers who they were, and then forgot how to speak.

prasangs.title_en: Sugriva: frightened, lifted, forgetful, forgiven
prasangs.summary: Sugriva, exiled and robbed by his brother, lives in fear even where Bali cannot reach him. Ram hears him and takes his side; after a first beating, Ram's touch takes the pain away, and Sugriva is made king. Then comfort makes him forget his promise to search for Sita. When he apologises, Ram smiles, says he is as dear as Bharat, and sends him back to work.
prasangs.lesson: Fear is heard, failure is forgiven, and then you get back to the work.
prasangs.story_hook: Even on the safest mountain in the kingdom, Sugriva jumped at every shadow.

prasangs.title_en: Bharat's love: the boon, the meeting, the sandals
prasangs.summary: Bharat, blamed for his mother's plot, asks the holy rivers for nothing but love for Ram, life after life; they tell him he torments himself for nothing. Walking toward Ram, shame slows him and remembering Ram's nature speeds him up. He falls at Ram's feet and Ram lifts him by force into an embrace. He returns with Ram's sandals and for fourteen years runs the kingdom from a hut, asking the sandals' leave for every task.
prasangs.lesson: Love can be lived as responsibility: do the work in the name of the one you love.
prasangs.story_hook: Everyone in Ayodhya assumed Bharat had schemed for the throne; he spent fourteen years proving them wrong from a hut.

prasangs.title_en: Sutikshna runs to meet Ram
prasangs.summary: A young sage hears Ram is near and runs out, sure he has no devotion, wisdom or discipline worth anything, trusting only that Ram loves those with nowhere else to go. Lost in love he wanders, dances, forgets the way; Ram watches from behind a tree, then lifts him up and holds him. Asked for a boon, the sage says only: may this one pride never leave me, that I am his.
prasangs.lesson: You don't have to feel qualified; the one with nowhere else to go is the one he loves.
prasangs.story_hook: A young sage ran out of his hut to meet Ram and, halfway there, forgot which way he was going.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman finds a devotee in Lanka
prasangs.summary: Searching Lanka by night, Hanuman wonders how a good person could live there, then hears someone wake saying 'Ram, Ram'. Vibhishan fears he has no practice or love worth Ram's notice; Hanuman, joking that no one wants to hear a monkey's name before breakfast, says that Ram showed kindness even to him, and weeps remembering it. The two talk of Ram late into the night and find a rest beyond words.
prasangs.lesson: In a hostile place, one friend who shares your faith can be enough.
prasangs.story_hook: In the middle of the enemy's city, at night, a monkey heard someone wake up and whisper the name of his Lord.

prasangs.title_en: Ram cannot repay Hanuman
prasangs.summary: Back from Lanka, Hanuman tells Ram how Sita survives: his name guards her day and night. Ram, in tears, asks whether one who relies on him can meet calamity; Hanuman answers that the only calamity is forgetting him. Ram says he can never repay Hanuman and cannot even look him in the face; Hanuman falls at his feet and will not get up. Offered anything, he asks only for unwavering devotion, and credits every deed to Ram.
prasangs.lesson: Do the work, give away the credit, and ask only to keep loving.
prasangs.story_hook: Hanuman had burned a city and found the queen; now he lay on the ground in front of Ram and refused to stand up.

prasangs.title_en: Valmiki: Hanuman's boon and Ram's debt
prasangs.summary: After the coronation Ram sends his friends home, asking only to be remembered with love. Hanuman asks to live as long as Ram's story is told, so that hearing it can ease his longing. Ram rises from the throne, embraces him, grants it, and says he would give his life for each of Hanuman's services, and hopes Hanuman never falls into trouble that would let him repay it.
prasangs.lesson: The deepest gratitude hopes the other never needs your help.
prasangs.story_hook: When the war was over and the guests were leaving, Hanuman asked Ram for the strangest gift: to keep hearing the story.

prasangs.title_en: Jayant the crow: shelter for the offender
prasangs.summary: Indra's son, disguised as a crow, pecks Sita's foot to test Ram's power. Ram's straw arrow chases him through every world; no god will shelter him. Narada sends him back to Ram, where he falls at his feet admitting he reaped what he sowed. Ram lets him go with the loss of one eye.
prasangs.lesson: Consequences may remain, but the one who turns back is still taken in.
prasangs.story_hook: The crow flew to heaven, to Shiva, to Brahma, and every door closed, until a sage told him to go back to the one he had wronged.

prasangs.title_en: Ram takes the spear meant for Vibhishan
prasangs.summary: In the final battle Ravana hurls a deadly spear at his brother Vibhishan. Remembering his vow to break the pain of those who come to him, Ram pushes Vibhishan behind him and takes the spear on himself.
prasangs.lesson: A promise of shelter is kept with one's own body.
prasangs.story_hook: The spear was aimed at the deserter; Ram stepped in front of it.

prasangs.title_en: The friends who couldn't leave
prasangs.summary: Vibhishan showers jewels from the flying chariot; the monkeys put them in their mouths and spit them out, and Ram, whom sages cannot reach in meditation, laughs with them. He thanks them, tells them to go home and remember him without fear. They stand weeping, unable to speak or leave, so he changes his plan and takes them all to Ayodhya.
prasangs.lesson: Pure love moves God more than any practice; it can even change his plans.
prasangs.story_hook: The war was won and the farewells said, but nobody moved.

prasangs.title_en: The child Ram and the crow
prasangs.summary: The crow-sage Kakbhushundi, after being humbled by the child Ram's play, receives his boon. Ram tells him devotees are always dear to him, that status counts for nothing without love, and gives the parable of a father with many gifted sons whose dearest son is the one who simply loves him, though skilled at nothing. Then the Lord goes back to being a hungry baby and cries until his mother runs to him.
prasangs.lesson: You are loved for loving, not for being impressive.
prasangs.story_hook: The Lord of all the worlds finished his great teaching to the crow, then scrunched up his face and started crying for his mother.

prasangs.title_en: Tulsidas's petition is signed
prasangs.summary: Tulsidas wrote the Vinay Patrika as a petition to Ram's court. In the last two padas he asks Hanuman, Bharat and Lakshman to mention him at the right moment. Lakshman, reading Hanuman's mind and Bharat's wish, speaks up: one servant has kept faith in the name even in this age. The court agrees, Ram smiles, says he has already taken note, and signs.
prasangs.lesson: After all the pleading, the book ends held: you were already noticed.
prasangs.story_hook: For 277 poems Tulsidas begged to be noticed; in the 279th, Ram picked up the pen.

prasangs.title_en: Tulsidas, the boy who begged for scraps
prasangs.summary: Across his later works Tulsidas tells his own story: left by his parents at birth, he wandered door to door for scraps, no job, no trade, no skill, ignored by everyone. Good people told him not to worry; Hanuman raised him like a child; Ram's name, he says, turned a thorny babul into a mango tree. Even when he went astray, he was taken back.
prasangs.lesson: Where you start is not where you end; you can be taken in from nothing.
prasangs.story_hook: The poet of the Ramcharitmanas began life as an unwanted child begging for scraps in the lanes.

prasangs.title_en: Shiva answers Parvati's doubt
prasangs.summary: Parvati, who in a past life as Sati doubted that a grieving prince could be God, now asks Shiva humbly: how can the formless one take a body? Shiva praises her question, bows to the child Ram, and answers that the formless becomes embodied out of love for devotees, and comes whenever good people suffer.
prasangs.lesson: Honest doubt, asked humbly, is welcomed; the answer is love.
prasangs.story_hook: Parvati had once lost everything by doubting quietly; this time she asked out loud.

prasangs.title_en: Ahalya: the long wait ends
prasangs.summary: On the way to Janakpur, Vishvamitra shows Ram a stone in an empty hermitage: Gautam's wife Ahalya, bearing a curse in a body of stone, longing for the dust of his feet. At his touch she rises, stands before him with folded hands, unable to speak for love, tears streaming, and asks only that her mind may always drink at his feet.
prasangs.lesson: However long you have been frozen, being seen can bring you back to life.
prasangs.story_hook: For years a stone lay in an abandoned hermitage, and only a sage knew it was a woman waiting.

prasangs.title_en: Draupadi's call and the single leaf of greens
prasangs.summary: Duryodhana sends the short-tempered sage Durvasa and ten thousand disciples to the exiled Pandavas after Draupadi has eaten and the sun-given pot is empty. With no way to feed them, Draupadi calls Krishna in her mind. He arrives at once, asks to be fed first, eats one leaf of greens stuck to the pot, and the sages, bathing in the river, suddenly feel full and flee.
prasangs.lesson: When you have nothing left to offer, calling out is enough; help can come from a single leaf.
prasangs.story_hook: The pot was scraped clean, and ten thousand hungry sages were bathing in the river, expecting dinner.

prasangs.title_en: Draupadi tells Krishna her sorrow
prasangs.summary: Krishna visits the exiled Pandavas in the Kamyaka forest and tells Arjuna 'you are mine and I am yours'. Draupadi then comes to him 'seeking refuge with the refuge', tells him, out of closeness, everything done to her in the dice-hall and since, and weeps that she has no one, not even him. Krishna promises she will see justice.
prasangs.lesson: You can bring God your rawest pain, even your sense of being abandoned, and be heard.
prasangs.story_hook: She came to him with her hair still unbound, thirteen years of humiliation in her voice.

prasangs.title_en: Krishna refuses the king's feast and eats at Vidura's house
